questions.title: Choosing Between #Temp Tables, Table Variables, and CTEs Inside a Stored Procedure
questions.prompt: You're writing a complex reporting stored procedure. Partway through, you compute an intermediate result set of roughly 200,000 rows that gets referenced three separate times later in the procedure, filtered differently each time, and would benefit from its own index on one of its columns. A junior developer on your team used a CTE for it because 'that's what we always use.' Explain why that choice is likely to hurt performance here, what you'd use instead and why, and the one scenario where a table variable would actually be the better choice over a temp table.
questions.modelAnswer:
A CTE isn't a stored, materialized result at all -- it's inlined into the statement that references it, and if you reference the same CTE three separate times, SQL Server may well re-run its underlying query three separate times (unless it happens to decide to spool the result on its own, which isn't something you can rely on or control). For a 200,000-row intermediate result referenced three times with different downstream filters, that risks recomputing the same expensive logic three times over, and a CTE also can't carry its own index -- so if the column you'd filter or join on isn't already well-served by indexes on the base tables, every one of those three references pays that cost independently.

A #temp table is the right choice here. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, which means two things that matter directly to this scenario: SQL Server maintains real statistics on it, so the optimizer can build a genuinely informed plan for each of the three later queries against it (rather than guessing), and you can explicitly CREATE INDEX on it -- so the column those three downstream queries filter or join on can actually be indexed, turning three potential scans into three seeks. At 200,000 rows, this is squarely the 'thousands of rows, reused more than once, might need its own index' case.

A table variable would be the better choice only when the intermediate set is small -- a handful to a few hundred rows -- and you're specifically trying to avoid statement recompilation inside a stored procedure. Historically, SQL Server assumed a table variable held exactly one row for costing purposes (pre-2019 compatibility levels, or without the newer deferred-compilation improvements), which is actually fine when the set really is tiny, but would badly under-allocate resources at 200,000 rows -- the opposite of what you want here. Table variables also aren't rolled back by an enclosing ROLLBACK, which occasionally matters for specific logging/auditing patterns, but that's a narrower reason to choose one and isn't the deciding factor in this scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior developer: the CTE choice makes sense as a habit, but it's working against them here specifically because of how many rows there are and how many times it gets used. A CTE doesn't actually store anything -- every time you reference it, SQL Server might just re-run the query behind it from scratch, and it has no index of its own. If we're touching this 200,000-row set three separate times with three different filters, we could be paying for that underlying computation three times, and none of those three references get to use an index on it even if one would help a lot.

My recommendation is a #temp table instead: dump that intermediate result into it once, put an index on whatever column the three downstream queries actually filter or join on, and now each of those three references gets a real seek against real statistics instead of SQL Server guessing. That's exactly the profile -- meaningful row count, reused multiple times, benefits from its own index -- where a temp table wins clearly.

I'd also tell them table variables aren't wrong, just wrong for this case -- they're great when the set is genuinely small and you're inside a procedure trying to avoid a recompile every time row counts shift. The catch is that SQL Server has historically assumed a table variable holds about one row when it's building a plan, which is totally fine for a small set but would be a disaster at 200,000 rows -- the optimizer would badly under-allocate for a set that size, and the plan quality would suffer for every one of those three references, not help it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a CTE out of habit regardless of row count or reuse pattern
Not realizing a CTE referenced multiple times may re-run its underlying query each time
Assuming a table variable always outperforms a temp table because it 'sounds lighter weight'
Putting a large, reused intermediate set into a table variable and getting a poor plan from the one-row cardinality assumption
Forgetting that only a #temp table supports an explicit CREATE INDEX statement after the fact
keyPoints: CTEs are inlined and re-evaluated per reference, not materialized or indexed
#Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and support explicit indexes
200,000 rows reused three times with filtering is a textbook #temp table case
Table variables historically get a one-row cardinality assumption, poor for large sets
Table variables fit small sets inside procedures where avoiding recompilation matters most

Recommends a #temp table and justifies it with statistics/indexing
Explains the risk of recomputation across three CTE references
Correctly identifies the scenario where a table variable wins
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Indexed Views: Mechanics and Restrictions
questions.prompt: Explain how an indexed view actually works under the hood in SQL Server — what SQL Server materializes, how it keeps that materialized data in sync with the base tables, and why indexed views come with such a strict list of requirements (deterministic functions only, no outer joins, SCHEMABINDING, etc.).
questions.modelAnswer: A standard view is just a stored query — nothing is persisted, and every time you select from it, SQL Server substitutes the view's definition into your query and compiles a plan against the base tables. An indexed view is fundamentally different: when you create a unique clustered index on a view, SQL Server actually materializes the result set of that view's query onto disk, in exactly the structure a clustered index implies (a b-tree with the data at the leaf level, physically sorted by the clustered index key). From that point on, the view's rows exist as real, maintained data, not a re-run query. Once that materialized data exists, SQL Server has to keep it transactionally consistent with the base tables, so every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against the underlying tables also triggers maintenance of the indexed view's data as part of the same transaction — this is handled automatically and synchronously, which is why indexed views add write overhead in proportion to how many views depend on the table. The strict rules exist precisely because this maintenance has to be deterministic and unambiguous: SCHEMABINDING is required so the base tables can't be altered out from under the view's materialized structure; aggregate functions need COUNT_BIG rather than COUNT so NULL/overflow semantics are unambiguous; outer joins and subqueries are disallowed because the engine can't always determine, incrementally, exactly which materialized rows need to change when a base row changes; and non-deterministic functions (GETDATE(), RAND()) are banned because the materialized value has to be reproducible and tied only to its deterministic inputs. In short, an indexed view trades write-time cost and a narrow set of allowed constructs for read-time speed, because the expensive aggregation or join work is done once at write time instead of on every read.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about indexed views is that they flip a normal view inside out. A regular view is lazy — it's just a saved SELECT statement, and the actual work happens every time someone queries it. An indexed view is the opposite: the moment you put a unique clustered index on it, SQL Server goes and physically builds that result set on disk, like any other table, and from then on it has to maintain it in real time. So if you've got an indexed view that aggregates sales by product, every single insert or update to the Sales table also updates that materialized aggregate behind the scenes, inside the same transaction. That's the trade-off — you're paying extra cost on every write so that reads against the view are basically free, just reading pre-computed data off disk instead of re-aggregating millions of rows. The restrictions make total sense once you see it that way — SCHEMABINDING locks the base tables so nobody can change a column type underneath the materialized structure, you need COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT because the engine needs predictable, deterministic math to maintain the aggregate incrementally, and things like outer joins or non-deterministic functions like GETDATE() are blocked because the engine genuinely can't figure out, row by row, exactly how to patch the materialized result when something changes upstream. I'd tell an interviewer: use indexed views when you have an expensive aggregate that's read far more often than the base data is written — that's the sweet spot — and be honest that they're not free, they add real overhead to every write against the underlying tables.
commonMistakes: Thinking an indexed view is 'just a view with an index for faster lookup' rather than a materialized, physically stored structure
Forgetting that maintenance happens synchronously inside the write transaction, not as an async refresh job
Not knowing why COUNT_BIG is mandatory instead of COUNT or COUNT(*)
Assuming indexed views support the same join/subquery flexibility as regular views
Overusing indexed views on heavy-write tables without weighing the write-amplification cost
keyPoints: Indexed views physically materialize the result set via a unique clustered index
Base table DML synchronously maintains the indexed view's data in the same transaction
SCHEMABINDING prevents base table changes that would break the materialized structure
Deterministic-only functions and no outer joins/subqueries are required for unambiguous incremental maintenance
The performance trade-off is faster reads at the cost of slower writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains physical materialization via unique clustered index
Explains synchronous maintenance on base table writes
Connects restrictions (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, no outer joins) to the underlying reason
Identifies the read-speed vs write-cost trade-off
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: Always Encrypted vs. Always Encrypted with Secure Enclaves: What Changes Under the Hood
questions.prompt: Explain how standard Always Encrypted actually protects data end-to-end, including what the driver does and what SQL Server itself is never allowed to see. Then explain specifically what a secure enclave adds, what becomes possible with enclaves that is impossible with standard Always Encrypted, and the trade-off a DBA takes on by enabling enclave-based computations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Standard Always Encrypted keeps plaintext data out of SQL Server's reach entirely, by design: a column designated as encrypted is encrypted client-side, inside the application's ODBC/JDBC driver (or ADO.NET provider) using a column encryption key the driver fetches and unwraps via a column master key, which typically lives somewhere outside the database entirely — a certificate store or Azure Key Vault. SQL Server stores and returns only ciphertext; it never possesses the keys needed to decrypt, so even a DBA with sysadmin rights querying the table directly sees encrypted binary values, not plaintext. This is what people mean by 'the database engine never sees the plaintext.' The cost of this design is real functional limits: SQL Server can perform equality comparisons against deterministically-encrypted columns (so WHERE EncryptedColumn = @value works, because identical plaintexts always produce identical ciphertext under deterministic encryption), but it cannot do range comparisons, pattern matching (LIKE), computations, or most built-in functions against encrypted columns at all, because the engine has no way to operate on ciphertext meaningfully — any such operation would have to happen client-side after decryption.

A secure enclave changes this by giving SQL Server a hardware- or software-isolated, attested region of memory where it can decrypt data temporarily and perform richer computation — pattern matching, range comparisons, in-place cryptographic operations for initial encryption or key rotation — without that plaintext ever being visible outside the enclave, including to the SQL Server process itself running outside the enclave boundary, the OS, or an administrator inspecting memory. The enclave proves its own integrity to the client driver via attestation before the driver will release keys into it, so the client isn't just trusting SQL Server's word that it's using an enclave correctly. This is what makes operations like server-side LIKE queries or in-place encryption of existing plaintext columns (without exporting data to a client app first) possible with enclaves but categorically impossible with standard Always Encrypted.

The trade-off: enabling enclave computations means trusting the enclave technology itself (and its attestation service — typically Microsoft Azure Attestation for Azure SQL) as part of your security boundary, which is a broader attack surface than 'the server never has the keys at all.' It also has real operational cost — enclave-enabled columns typically require the newer 'randomized encryption with enclave computations' and specific driver/compatibility-level support, and attestation adds a dependency and a potential availability/latency factor that doesn't exist in the simpler, zero-trust-in-server model. A DBA choosing enclaves is deliberately trading a small amount of additional trusted surface area for meaningfully richer query capability against encrypted data.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd explain standard Always Encrypted is: the server is completely blind. Encryption and decryption happen in the client driver, the keys live outside SQL Server — often in Key Vault — and all SQL Server ever sees or stores is ciphertext. That's true even for me as a DBA with full admin rights; I can query the table directly and all I get back is encrypted bytes. The catch is that blindness has a cost — SQL Server can do an equality check against deterministically-encrypted data because identical plaintext always maps to identical ciphertext, but it can't do a range filter, a LIKE, or run any function against that column, because it genuinely cannot operate meaningfully on ciphertext it can't read.

A secure enclave is Microsoft's answer to that limitation — it's a protected, attested little sandbox inside the server where SQL Server actually can decrypt and compute on real data temporarily, without that plaintext ever leaking out to the rest of the SQL Server process, the OS, or anyone looking at memory from outside. The attestation piece matters a lot to me — the client driver doesn't just take SQL Server's word that there's a legitimate enclave running; it gets cryptographic proof from an attestation service before it'll even hand over the keys. That's what unlocks things that are flatly impossible otherwise, like running a LIKE against encrypted data server-side, or doing in-place encryption of a column that already has plaintext data in it without having to round-trip every row through a client app first.

The trade-off I'd be upfront about with a security team: you're adding a little bit of trusted surface area back in — you now have to trust the enclave hardware/software and the attestation service — in exchange for real query flexibility. It's not free, and there's real setup overhead around attestation and driver/compatibility requirements, but for a lot of real applications, giving up the absolute zero-trust-in-server guarantee for workable range queries and pattern matching is worth it.
commonMistakes: Believing a DBA with sysadmin rights can read Always Encrypted plaintext directly from the table
Assuming any WHERE clause works against an Always Encrypted column, not just deterministic equality
Thinking secure enclaves eliminate the need for column/master key management
Not understanding that attestation is what prevents a compromised server from faking enclave behavior
Treating enclave-based Always Encrypted as strictly more secure rather than a different trust trade-off
keyPoints: Standard Always Encrypted decrypts only in the client driver; SQL Server stores and sees only ciphertext
Deterministic encryption allows equality comparisons server-side; randomized encryption doesn't even allow that
Range queries, LIKE, and computations are impossible against standard Always Encrypted columns
Secure enclaves give SQL Server an attested, isolated region to decrypt and compute without exposing plaintext elsewhere
Attestation (e.g., Azure Attestation) proves enclave integrity to the client before keys are released
Enclaves trade a small increase in trusted surface area for richer server-side query capability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains standard Always Encrypted's client-side-only decryption model
Correctly distinguishes deterministic equality support from other operations being impossible
Correctly explains what a secure enclave adds and how attestation works
Correctly articulates the trust/trade-off of enabling enclaves
Clarity and precision

questions.title: Dynamic Data Masking: What It Actually Protects Against, and What It Doesn't
questions.prompt: A compliance officer wants Dynamic Data Masking applied to a CustomerSSN column and believes this 'encrypts' the data so it's protected at rest. Correct this misunderstanding: explain exactly what DDM does and does not do, at what layer it operates, and describe a specific, realistic way a user with ad-hoc query access could still exfiltrate the real unmasked values despite DDM being configured.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dynamic Data Masking is a presentation-layer control, not an encryption or at-rest protection mechanism. The actual bytes stored on disk for CustomerSSN are completely unchanged, in plaintext (or whatever encryption is separately applied, like TDE, which protects the physical files but not query results) — DDM only intercepts the result set returned to a query and substitutes a masking function's output for users who are not explicitly exempted from masking (members of db_owner, or any role/user granted the UNMASK permission, see the real value). This means DDM provides zero protection against anyone with sufficient permission to run arbitrary queries and who either already has UNMASK, is in db_owner, or who can get the underlying data to leave the masked column entirely.

A realistic exfiltration path despite DDM being configured: a user with ordinary SELECT permission (not UNMASK) runs a query that moves the SSN value through an expression before it's returned, for example SELECT CustomerSSN + '' or CAST(CustomerSSN AS varchar) concatenated with another column, or uses the value in a WHERE clause with a known candidate value — DDM is documented to be bypassable via inference attacks using range queries or brute-force guessing against a predictable value (a 9-digit SSN has, at most, a billion possibilities, and many fewer in practice given format rules), where the attacker repeatedly queries WHERE CustomerSSN = '<guess>' and observes whether a row is returned, narrowing down the real value without ever seeing it unmasked directly. Microsoft's own documentation explicitly warns DDM is not a substitute for proper access control or encryption and should always be combined with least-privilege permissions, auditing, and (for truly sensitive fields like SSN) Always Encrypted or column-level encryption if the goal is to actually prevent the value from being readable by unauthorized principals at all, including privileged ones.

So the correction for the compliance officer: DDM reduces accidental over-exposure for everyday users and reporting tools who have no business reason to see raw SSNs, but it is not encryption, doesn't protect data at rest, and does not stop a determined or sufficiently-privileged user from recovering the real value — either by being granted UNMASK, being in db_owner, or through inference/brute-force querying. For data this sensitive, DDM should be paired with, not substituted for, Always Encrypted and strict least-privilege access.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk the compliance officer back from 'encrypts' pretty directly: DDM doesn't touch the actual bytes on disk at all — the real SSN is sitting there completely unchanged, it's only the result set coming back from a query that gets substituted with a masked pattern, and only for users who aren't already exempt. Db_owners and anyone granted UNMASK see the real value every time, full stop.

To make it concrete, I'd show them this: take a user with plain SELECT access on the table, no UNMASK. They can't just select the column and see the SSN — fine. But they can run something like WHERE CustomerSSN = '123-45-6789' and watch whether a row comes back. Do that enough times with different guesses, and you can brute-force or narrow down the real SSN without ever seeing an unmasked value directly — that's a documented, known limitation of DDM, and Microsoft themselves say explicitly it's not meant to replace real encryption or access control.

What I'd recommend instead for something this sensitive: keep DDM if they want it for day-to-day protection against accidental over-exposure in reports and ad-hoc queries by people who have no reason to see raw SSNs, but for actual protection against a privileged or determined user recovering the value, they need Always Encrypted on that column and tightly scoped, audited access — DDM alone is not the control that gets them compliant for something like SSNs.
commonMistakes: Believing DDM encrypts the underlying data
Assuming DDM protects against any user with SELECT permission, not just non-exempt users
Not recognizing the WHERE-clause inference/brute-force bypass as a real, documented risk
Treating DDM as sufficient compliance control for highly sensitive fields like SSNs on its own
Forgetting that TDE (at rest) and DDM (presentation) solve completely different problems
keyPoints: DDM only changes what's returned in a query result set, not the underlying stored bytes
db_owner members and anyone with UNMASK permission always see real, unmasked values
DDM provides no protection for data at rest; that's a separate concern (TDE, encryption)
DDM is bypassable via inference/brute-force attacks using WHERE clause guessing
Microsoft explicitly documents DDM as a presentation control, not a substitute for encryption or access control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains DDM operates only on query result sets, not stored data
Correctly identifies who bypasses masking (db_owner, UNMASK) by default
Describes a concrete, realistic bypass/exfiltration method
Recommends appropriate complementary controls (Always Encrypted, least privilege)
Clarity in correcting the compliance officer's misunderstanding

questions.title: RPO and RTO: Translating Business Requirements Into an Actual HA/DR Design
questions.prompt: Define Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective precisely, in a way that distinguishes them from each other without ambiguity. Then explain why a business stakeholder saying 'we can't lose any data and we need to be back up instantly' is not actually an RPO/RTO requirement yet, and what you, as the DBA, need to get from them before you can pick between options like geo-replication, failover groups, and Always On Availability Groups.
questions.modelAnswer:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) answers: how much data, measured in time, are we willing to lose if a failure happens right now? If RPO is 5 minutes, it means the business accepts that in a disaster, up to 5 minutes of the most recent transactions might not exist in the recovered system — it's a measure of acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window, not a measure of speed. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) answers a completely different question: how long are we willing to be down — from the moment of failure to the moment the system is usable again? RTO is a measure of acceptable downtime duration, and it says nothing about how much data is in the system once it's back. These two numbers are independent: you can have a near-zero RPO (synchronous replication, no committed transaction is lost) paired with a long RTO (failover takes 30 minutes to execute and validate), or a long RPO (hourly snapshot backups) paired with a short RTO (restoring that snapshot is fast), or any other combination — one doesn't imply the other.

'We can't lose any data and need to be back up instantly' sounds like RPO=0 and RTO=0, but it's not a usable requirement yet because it hasn't been tested against reality or cost: true RPO=0 requires synchronous replication, which has real latency and throughput cost and specific failure-mode implications (if the secondary isn't reachable, do writes block, or does the primary continue async and risk data loss anyway?); true RTO≈0 requires automatic failover with health detection fast enough that applications barely notice, which costs more in infrastructure (multiple always-on replicas, likely cross-region) and still has some non-zero floor given DNS/connection-string propagation and application reconnection behavior. Until the stakeholder has actually weighed that cost and those trade-offs, 'zero and instant' is really just 'this is extremely important to us,' not a specified, costed number.

What I need from them before I can choose an architecture: a realistic, specific number for each — in minutes, not adjectives — ideally tied to what a real outage would cost per minute of downtime and per unit of data loss, so the number reflects actual business impact rather than an unexamined ideal. I also need to know the acceptable failure scope (single server, whole region, whole Azure outage) and whether they need this in a different geographic region (which pushes toward active geo-replication / auto-failover groups, inherently asynchronous across regions due to physics) versus same-region/zone (which allows synchronous Always On AG replicas with near-zero RPO). Only with real numbers and failure scope can I actually recommend, for example, Always On AG with a synchronous secondary in the same region for RTO measured in seconds and RPO near zero against a server/zone failure, versus auto-failover groups with geo-replication to a different region for surviving a full regional outage, where RPO will realistically be some small non-zero number because cross-region replication is asynchronous.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain RPO and RTO as answering two completely separate questions, and I always walk through both definitions explicitly because people genuinely conflate them. RPO is about data — if disaster strikes this second, how far back in time are we willing for our restored data to be? RTO is about time to recovery — from the moment things break, how long can the business tolerate being down before it's back up and usable? Neither one tells you anything about the other; you could be down for an hour but lose zero data, or be back up in thirty seconds but lose the last five minutes of transactions.

When a stakeholder says 'zero data loss, instant recovery,' I don't push back on the sentiment — that's clearly how important this system is to them — but I do push back on treating that as an actual spec, because it hasn't been priced or tested yet. True zero RPO means synchronous replication, which has real latency cost on every write and real decisions to make about what happens if the secondary goes unreachable. True zero RTO means automated failover fast enough that nobody notices, which means paying for standby capacity that's basically always running. Until they've seen what that costs and traded it off against the actual cost of an outage, 'instant and zero' is an aspiration, not a number I can design against.

So before I pick anything, I'm asking them for two real numbers in minutes — tied ideally to what an outage actually costs them per minute — and I'm asking what kind of failure they're protecting against: a single server dying, or an entire Azure region going dark. If it's same-region, I can get them close to zero RPO and a fast RTO with Always On AG synchronous replicas. If they genuinely need to survive a whole region disappearing, I'm talking about auto-failover groups with geo-replication, and I'll tell them upfront that cross-region replication is inherently asynchronous, so RPO in that scenario won't be a true zero no matter what we buy — it'll be small, but not zero, and I want them to agree to that number deliberately rather than discover it during a real outage.
commonMistakes: Treating RPO and RTO as the same concept or using them interchangeably
Accepting 'zero data loss, instant recovery' as a design spec without quantifying cost/trade-offs
Assuming synchronous replication is free or has no latency implications
Believing geo-replication across regions can achieve true zero RPO
Designing an HA/DR architecture before establishing the actual failure scope the business needs to survive
keyPoints: RPO measures acceptable data loss as a time window; RTO measures acceptable downtime duration
RPO and RTO are independent of each other and must be specified separately
'Zero and instant' is an aspiration, not a costed requirement, until trade-offs are examined
True near-zero RPO requires synchronous replication with real latency/throughput cost
Cross-region (geo) replication is inherently asynchronous, so cross-region RPO is never truly zero
Failure scope (server, zone, region) determines whether AG, failover groups, or geo-replication fits

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly and precisely defines RPO and RTO as distinct measures
Explains why the stated requirement isn't yet actionable/costed
Identifies the specific information needed (numbers, failure scope) before designing
Correctly maps failure scope to AG vs. failover groups/geo-replication
Clarity and business-communication framing

questions.title: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication: What Actually Changes
questions.prompt: Explain the real architectural difference between SQL Authentication and Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication against Azure SQL Database — not just 'one uses a password and one uses Azure AD,' but what each one means for credential storage, token lifetime, conditional access, and auditability. Then explain why a security-conscious DBA would push to eliminate SQL Authentication logins entirely wherever possible.
questions.modelAnswer:
SQL Authentication is self-contained within SQL Server/Azure SQL: a login's password hash is stored in the master database (or, for contained database users, in the user database itself), the server validates the password directly against that stored hash, and there is no external identity system involved at all — the credential's entire lifecycle (creation, rotation, expiration policy, lockout) is managed by SQL Server itself, with no integration into any organization-wide identity governance.

Microsoft Entra authentication is fundamentally different: the user or application authenticates against Entra ID first, and Azure SQL never sees a password at all — it receives and validates a signed, time-limited access token issued by Entra, which asserts the caller's identity and group memberships. This has several concrete consequences. Credential storage moves entirely out of the database: there's no password hash sitting in master to protect or leak. Token lifetime means access is inherently time-boxed — a stolen or cached token expires on its own schedule (commonly around an hour, with refresh tokens subject to the organization's own session policies), unlike a SQL login's password, which is valid indefinitely until someone manually changes it. Conditional Access becomes possible for database access specifically because Entra sits in the authentication path: an organization can require multi-factor authentication, block sign-in from untrusted locations or unmanaged devices, or require a compliant device, all enforced before Entra ever issues the token Azure SQL will accept — none of that is possible for a SQL login, which only ever checks a password. And auditability improves because every authentication event ties back to a real organizational identity in Entra (and can be correlated with Entra's own sign-in logs, MFA challenges, and Conditional Access evaluation results), rather than a shared or service-style SQL login whose actual human (or service) user may not be individually distinguishable in SQL Server's own audit trail.

A security-conscious DBA pushes to eliminate SQL Authentication logins wherever possible because every one of those benefits is simply unavailable to a password-based login: passwords can be shared, written down, reused across systems, phished, or brute-forced with no MFA in the way; a compromised SQL login's password keeps working until someone notices and manually rotates it, with no automatic expiration; and there's no way to apply Conditional Access policies to a bare SQL login no matter how mature the organization's Entra security posture is elsewhere. Realistically, SQL Authentication logins usually survive only for specific legacy application compatibility cases or non-Entra-aware tooling — everything else should move to Entra-based access, ideally through managed identities for applications and Entra groups for human access, so that joiner/mover/leaver identity lifecycle and access reviews happen through the organization's existing identity governance instead of being a separate, DBA-maintained password list.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always frame this as: SQL Authentication is the database being its own entire identity system, and Entra authentication is the database deliberately outsourcing that job to the organization's actual identity provider. With SQL auth, the password hash lives right there in master, SQL Server itself checks it, and that's the whole story — no outside system is involved, which also means no outside system's protections apply either.

With Entra auth, Azure SQL never even sees a password — it's handed a signed token that Entra already vouched for, and that token expires on its own, usually within about an hour. That short lifetime alone is a big deal operationally — a SQL login's password is valid forever until a human remembers to rotate it, but a leaked Entra token is only useful for a limited window. And because Entra sits in front of the whole thing, I can get Conditional Access in the picture — requiring MFA, blocking sign-in from outside the corporate network or from a device that isn't compliant — none of which is even a concept SQL Authentication understands, because it's just checking a password against a hash.

Auditability is the other piece I always bring up — with Entra, every connection ties back to a real identity I can trace through Entra's own sign-in logs, correlated with MFA and Conditional Access decisions. A shared SQL login, by contrast, is a black box — everyone using it looks identical in the logs.

So when I'm pushing to kill off SQL logins, it's not about SQL Authentication being 'weak' in isolation — a strong password with proper rotation is still a password — it's that it structurally can't plug into any of the organization's broader identity security investment. No MFA, no Conditional Access, no automatic expiration, no real per-person auditability. I'll keep a SQL login around only when something genuinely can't speak Entra, and even then I treat it as a tracked exception, not the default.
commonMistakes: Describing the difference as only 'passwords vs. Azure AD' without explaining the token/Conditional Access mechanics
Assuming MFA or Conditional Access can somehow be applied to a SQL login
Believing SQL Authentication passwords expire or rotate automatically the way Entra tokens do
Not recognizing that shared/service SQL logins degrade individual auditability
Assuming eliminating all SQL logins is always possible regardless of legacy application constraints
keyPoints: SQL Authentication stores and validates password hashes entirely within SQL Server, with no external identity involved
Entra authentication validates a signed, time-limited token issued by Entra; Azure SQL never sees a password
Conditional Access (MFA, device compliance, location) can only be enforced through Entra, never through SQL logins
Token-based access is inherently time-boxed, unlike indefinitely-valid SQL login passwords
Entra-based access ties to a real identity in centralized sign-in/audit logs; shared SQL logins obscure who actually connected

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the credential storage/validation difference
Correctly explains token lifetime implications
Correctly explains why Conditional Access only applies via Entra

questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ROW_NUMBER/PARTITION BY/DELETE query
Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Covering, Filtered Index for a High-Frequency Reporting Query
questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint runs this query hundreds of times per minute: SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product WHERE Color = 'Red' AND SellEndDate IS NULL ORDER BY ListPrice. Design the single nonclustered index you'd create to best serve it -- specifying key column order, included columns, and any filter -- and explain exactly how you'd confirm in the execution plan that it's actually being used as a fully covering seek rather than falling back to a scan or a key lookup.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query filters on Color (equality) and SellEndDate IS NULL, then orders by ListPrice, and selects ProductID, Name, ListPrice. I'd build the index key on Color first, since it's the equality predicate the optimizer can seek on directly, then ListPrice second, since that both satisfies part of the ORDER BY and keeps rows pre-sorted within each color -- letting the engine potentially avoid a separate sort operator entirely. ProductID and Name don't belong in the key at all; they're only ever selected, never filtered or sorted on, so they belong as INCLUDE columns, which attaches their data to the index's leaf level without making them part of the search key (keeping the key itself narrow). Finally, since this query only ever cares about currently-active products, I'd add a filter: WHERE SellEndDate IS NULL, so the index only covers the subset of rows this specific query pattern actually needs -- smaller, faster to scan, and still perfectly usable by any other query matching that same filter condition.

To confirm it's working as intended, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run the exact production query. I'm looking for a single Index Seek operator with no accompanying Key Lookup and no separate Sort operator afterward -- that combination means the index is fully covering (every selected column came straight from the index, no trip back to the clustered index) and pre-sorted for the ORDER BY. If I instead see an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup, that tells me I missed an included column the query actually needs. If I see a Sort operator after the seek, either my key column order doesn't match the ORDER BY the way I assumed, or the optimizer decided sorting was cheaper than using the index's physical order for some other reason. And if I see a Scan instead of a Seek at all, I'd first check that the filter predicate on the index exactly matches the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server will only use a filtered index when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter, and a subtle mismatch (like comparing against a variable instead of a literal in some SQL Server versions) can silently prevent that match and fall back to scanning the base table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through the query, I see one equality filter (Color), one IS NULL filter that's really describing 'currently active products' (SellEndDate), an ORDER BY on ListPrice, and three columns actually being selected. So my index key is Color first, because that's the equality predicate, then ListPrice second, because that handles the sort and keeps things grouped nicely within each color. ProductID and Name never show up in a WHERE or ORDER BY here, so I don't want them cluttering the key -- they go in as INCLUDE columns instead, just along for the ride so the index can hand back the full row without touching the base table. And since this query only ever wants active products, I'd make the whole index filtered on SellEndDate IS NULL -- there's no reason to carry the weight of retired products in an index built specifically for this access pattern.

To prove it's actually helping, I turn on the actual plan and run the real query, and I want to see exactly one operator: an Index Seek, nothing else hanging off it. If there's a Key Lookup tagging along, that tells me I forgot to include a column the query needed. If there's a Sort sitting after the seek, my key order isn't lining up with the ORDER BY the way I thought it would. And if I'm staring at a Scan instead of a Seek, my first suspicion is that the filter on the index doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server is strict about that match for a filtered index, and small mismatches are a classic reason the optimizer quietly falls back to ignoring it.
commonMistakes: Putting ProductID/Name in the index key instead of as INCLUDE columns, widening the key unnecessarily
Forgetting the ORDER BY column when choosing key column order, leaving a Sort in the plan
Leaving off the filter, indexing retired products the query never actually needs
Assuming an Index Seek alone proves full coverage without checking for an accompanying Key Lookup
Writing a filter predicate that doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause, causing SQL Server to ignore the filtered index
keyPoints: Equality predicate columns go first in the index key, ahead of sort/range columns
ORDER BY columns in the key can eliminate a separate Sort operator
Select-only columns belong in INCLUDE, not the key, to keep the key narrow
A filtered index should match the query's WHERE clause as closely as possible
Verify with the actual execution plan: single seek, no Key Lookup, no Sort = fully covering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct key column choice and order (Color, ListPrice)
Correctly places ProductID/Name as INCLUDE columns
Correctly applies the SellEndDate IS NULL filter
Describes verifying via actual execution plan (seek, no key lookup, no sort)
Explains what a Key Lookup or Sort in the plan would each indicate is wrong

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';
commonMistakes: Only fixing one of the two predicates and leaving the other non-SARGable branch in the OR
Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies both predicates as non-SARGable and explains why
Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Uses a half-open interval that correctly handles time components
Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
Clean, correct SQL syntax

questions.title: Configuring Dynamic Data Masking with T-SQL on an Existing Table
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL to add Dynamic Data Masking to an existing Customers table: mask the Email column with the email masking function, mask the Phone column with a custom partial mask that shows only the last 4 digits, and mask SSN with the default masking function. Then write the T-SQL to grant a reporting role the ability to see unmasked SSN values without granting it broader permissions, and the T-SQL to verify a non-privileged login actually sees masked output.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each masking rule is applied with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = '...'), which attaches the masking metadata to the column without altering its data type or the underlying stored value. The email function (default()) specifically formats as the first letter plus XXX@XXX.com regardless of the real value's structure. For Phone, a partial mask gives control over exactly how many leading/trailing characters show and what fills the middle: partial(0,'XXX-XXX-',4) shows zero characters at the start, then the literal padding, then the last 4 real characters -- which satisfies 'only the last 4 digits' precisely. SSN uses the generic default() mask, which for a string type returns a fixed-length XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX regardless of the real value's actual length or content, which is the standard, un-customized obfuscation Microsoft documents for default().

Granting unmask access without broader permissions is done with GRANT UNMASK TO <role>, which is a narrow, standalone permission -- it does not imply or require db_owner, SELECT, or any other grant, and it can be revoked independently with REVOKE UNMASK. This is the deliberate design: UNMASK only affects whether masking is applied to values a principal is already otherwise permitted to see through other grants; it doesn't grant read access on its own.

To verify a non-privileged login actually sees masked output, I'd use EXECUTE AS USER = '<login_name>' (requiring IMPERSONATE permission, or just testing with an actual separate low-privilege connection) to run the SELECT as that identity, confirm the masked pattern appears instead of real values, then REVERT back to my own session -- running the SELECT as myself (likely db_owner or sysadmin) would be meaningless since those roles always bypass masking regardless of any DDM configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd handle each column with its own ALTER TABLE ... ADD MASKED WITH statement -- that's the whole mechanism, and it's non-destructive, it just tags the column with masking metadata, the real value underneath never changes. For email I'd use the built-in email() function since that's exactly what it's designed for. For phone, since the requirement is specifically 'only show the last 4 digits,' I reach for partial() and set it up so zero characters show at the start, I control what the padding looks like in the middle, and exactly 4 real characters show at the end. For SSN, default() is the right call since there's no customization requested -- it just gives the standard fixed masked pattern for that data type.

For the reporting role needing to see real SSNs, I'd specifically avoid reaching for anything broader than GRANT UNMASK TO that role -- that permission exists precisely so I'm not forced to hand out db_owner or extra SELECT grants just to unmask a column, and I can pull it back cleanly later with REVOKE UNMASK if their need changes.

And to actually prove this works rather than just assume it, I always test as the actual low-privilege identity -- either a real separate connection logged in as that user, or EXECUTE AS USER if I have IMPERSONATE rights, run the exact SELECT, and confirm I'm seeing the masked pattern, not the real data. I wouldn't trust testing this under my own session, because as db_owner or sysadmin I'd see real values regardless of what masking is configured -- that's not a meaningful test of what DDM is actually doing for everyone else.
commonMistakes: Assuming ADD MASKED WITH changes the actual stored value
Using default() for phone when the requirement calls for a specific partial mask
Granting db_owner or broad SELECT instead of the narrow UNMASK permission
Testing masked behavior under a sysadmin/db_owner session, which always bypasses masking
Forgetting GRANT UNMASK can be scoped and later revoked independently
keyPoints: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH attaches masking without changing stored data
partial() mask gives explicit control over prefix/suffix character counts and padding
GRANT UNMASK is a standalone permission, independent of SELECT/db_owner
UNMASK only affects masking, not underlying read access, which must already be granted separately
Testing masked output must be done as the actual non-privileged principal, not as db_owner/sysadmin

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DDM syntax for all three columns (email, custom partial phone, default SSN)
Correct GRANT UNMASK statement scoped narrowly to the reporting role
Correct verification method using a non-privileged identity
Explains why db_owner/sysadmin testing is invalid

questions.title: Query Store: Finding and Force-Fixing a Regressed Query Plan
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL against Query Store's catalog views to find queries whose average duration has gotten at least 3x worse in the last day compared to the prior week, and then write the T-SQL to force the better of two known plans for the worst offender. Explain what forcing a plan actually does and does not guarantee going forward.
questions.modelAnswer:
Query Store exposes per-plan, per-time-interval runtime statistics in sys.query_store_runtime_stats, linked to sys.query_store_plan (which plan), sys.query_store_query (which logical query), and sys.query_store_query_text (the actual text), bucketed by sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval. To find regressions, I aggregate average duration for a recent interval (last 24 hours) and compare it against the average for an earlier baseline interval (the prior week), joining on query_id, and filter to where recent_avg >= 3 * baseline_avg. This requires being careful to aggregate avg_duration weighted by execution count (or just compare straight averages if execution counts are roughly comparable) across potentially multiple plans and multiple runtime_stats_interval rows per plan within each time window.

Once I've identified the worst offender's query_id, I'd look at sys.query_store_plan for that query_id to find a known-good historical plan_id (one whose historical average duration was much better), and then call sys.sp_query_store_force_plan (@query_id, @plan_id) to force it.

Forcing a plan guarantees the optimizer will use that specific plan shape for that query going forward -- it pins the plan rather than letting the optimizer re-choose, as long as the plan remains valid (the schema hasn't changed in a way that invalidates it, e.g., a referenced index being dropped). It does NOT guarantee that plan will stay optimal forever: if the underlying data distribution shifts significantly (a table grows 50x, or a previously rare value becomes extremely common), the forced plan can become the wrong choice again, and forcing doesn't adapt to that -- it has to be manually revisited. It also does not retroactively fix already-cached bad plans elsewhere unless they share the same query_id/plan_id mechanism, and it's a per-query action, not a global, set-it-and-forget-it fix, so I'd still want monitoring in place (re-running this same regression query periodically) to catch when a forced plan itself eventually becomes the regression.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My approach is to go straight at Query Store's runtime stats views -- that's literally what they're there for. I pull average duration for the most recent day and the prior week, grouped by query_id, and look for anywhere the recent number is at least three times worse than the baseline. I have to be a little careful joining across sys.query_store_runtime_stats and its interval table since a query can have multiple plans and multiple time buckets, but the core idea is just comparing two averages.

Once I've got the worst offender's query_id, I go look at its plan history in sys.query_store_plan to find a plan_id that used to perform well, and then I force it with sp_query_store_force_plan -- one call, two parameters, query_id and plan_id.

The thing I always make sure people understand about forcing a plan: it's not magic, and it's not permanent protection. What it actually does is pin the optimizer to use that specific plan shape going forward, as long as that plan is still valid -- if someone drops an index the plan depends on, forcing breaks and SQL Server falls back to choosing a new plan. What it doesn't do is adapt if the data itself changes dramatically later -- if that table grows fifty times bigger, the plan I forced today because it was fast might become the wrong choice six months from now, and forcing won't notice that on its own. It's a targeted fix for right now, not a forever guarantee, so I'd keep re-running this regression check periodically rather than treating one force_plan call as the end of the story.
questions.example:
SELECT q.query_id, AVG(rs.avg_duration) AS avg_dur
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval rsi ON rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = rsi.runtime_stats_interval_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query q ON p.query_id = q.query_id
WHERE rsi.start_time >= DATEADD(DAY, -1, SYSUTCDATETIME())
GROUP BY q.query_id;

-- Force the better known plan:
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 482, @plan_id = 519;
commonMistakes: Comparing total duration instead of average duration, skewing results by execution count
Not joining through the interval table, mixing up time windows incorrectly
Assuming sp_query_store_force_plan permanently guarantees good performance regardless of future data changes
Forcing a plan without first confirming it actually performed better historically
Treating a single force_plan action as a substitute for ongoing monitoring
keyPoints: Regression detection compares recent average duration against a prior baseline per query_id
sys.query_store_runtime_stats joined with plan/query/text catalog views provides the needed data
sp_query_store_force_plan pins a specific plan_id for a query_id going forward
Forcing a plan does not adapt to future data distribution changes
Forcing only remains effective while the plan stays valid (e.g., referenced indexes still exist)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct regression-detection query using Query Store catalog views
Correct use of sp_query_store_force_plan with appropriate query_id/plan_id
Correctly explains what forcing a plan guarantees
Correctly explains what forcing a plan does NOT guarantee (data drift, validity)

questions.title: Configuring an Auto-Failover Group Between Two Azure SQL Servers
questions.prompt: Write the Azure CLI commands to create an auto-failover group named sales-fg between a primary logical server in East US and a secondary logical server already provisioned in West US, add an existing database to it, and set a grace period of 2 hours before automatic failover triggers. Then explain what actually happens to client connection strings during a failover, and why the grace period setting matters for avoiding unnecessary failovers.
questions.modelAnswer:
The az sql failover-group create command establishes the group, specifying the primary server, the partner (secondary) server, which must already exist with appropriate networking/replication prerequisites, and the list of databases to add. The --failover-policy Automatic with --grace-period (in hours) controls the automatic-failover behavior; add-db (or specifying databases at creation) associates the specific database(s) with the group so their geo-replication and failover are managed as a unit rather than per-database manually.

What actually happens to client connections during a failover: the failover group exposes a special, stable listener endpoint -- a DNS name distinct from either individual server's own endpoint (something like sales-fg.database.windows.net) -- and applications should connect to that listener endpoint, never to the primary server's own hostname directly. When a failover occurs (automatic or manual), Azure updates where that listener's DNS name resolves to, pointing it at the new primary (the former secondary). Existing open connections to the old primary are dropped and must be re-established by the application (most connection pooling/retry logic in a well-written client handles this with a reconnect), but new connections made after DNS propagation automatically land on the new primary without any connection string change in the application's configuration -- that's the entire point of using the listener endpoint instead of a server-specific name.

The grace period matters because automatic failover is triggered based on an outage being sustained for at least that long, not on any single failed health check -- a 2-hour grace period means a transient blip (a brief network partition, a short Azure-side incident that self-resolves in 20 minutes) will NOT trigger a failover, because the outage didn't persist long enough to cross the threshold. This avoids the costly and disruptive scenario of failing over for a problem that would have resolved on its own, since failing over has real costs: a failover and its eventual failback both involve DNS propagation delay, a window where applications are reconnecting, and depending on replication lag at the moment of failover, a small risk of data loss for any transactions not yet replicated to the secondary (geo-replication is asynchronous). Setting the grace period too short risks unnecessary failovers for transient issues; setting it too long delays recovery from a genuinely sustained outage beyond what the business's actual RTO tolerates -- so the number has to be chosen deliberately against the RTO requirement, not left at a default without thought.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd run az sql failover-group create against the primary server, pointing it at the already-provisioned secondary in West US as the partner server, and add the specific database to the group in that same step. For the automatic policy, I'd set failover-policy to Automatic and grace-period to 2, which is in hours.

The piece I always make sure people understand about failover groups is the listener endpoint -- there's a separate DNS name for the group itself, not either server's own hostname, and that's what every application connection string should actually point to. When a failover happens, Azure flips what that listener name resolves to, pointing it at the new primary. Existing connections that were open against the old primary get dropped and have to reconnect -- that's just how TCP connections work when the underlying server changes -- but as long as the app is pointed at the listener name and has reasonable retry logic, it reconnects to the right place automatically with zero config changes on the application side.

And the grace period is there specifically to stop a failover group from overreacting to something that was never a real outage. Two hours means a 20-minute blip that resolves on its own never triggers anything -- the failover policy requires the problem to persist across that whole window first. That matters because failing over isn't free: there's DNS propagation time, a reconnect storm while apps catch up, and because geo-replication is asynchronous, there's a real possibility of losing whatever transactions hadn't replicated yet at the moment of the actual failover. So I'd tell a team: don't just leave the grace period at some default, pick it deliberately against your actual RTO -- too short and you're failing over for things that would've fixed themselves, too long and a real outage drags on past what the business said it could tolerate.
questions.example:
az sql failover-group create \
  --name sales-fg \
  --partner-server west-us-secondary \
  --server east-us-primary \
  --resource-group rg-sales-db \
  --failover-policy Automatic \
  --grace-period 2 \
  --add-db SalesDB
commonMistakes: Pointing application connection strings at the primary server's own hostname instead of the listener endpoint
Assuming existing open connections survive a failover without reconnecting
Setting grace period to zero or a very short value without considering transient-outage false triggers
Believing automatic failover guarantees zero data loss regardless of grace period or replication lag
Forgetting the secondary server/networking prerequisites must already exist before creating the group
keyPoints: az sql failover-group create establishes the group with primary, partner server, and member databases
Applications must connect to the failover group's listener endpoint, not a server-specific hostname
Failover re-points the listener's DNS; new connections land on the new primary automatically
Existing connections are dropped and must reconnect; well-written clients handle this via retry logic
Grace period requires the outage to persist that long before triggering, avoiding failover for transient blips
Failover has real cost (reconnect disruption, possible async-replication data loss) so grace period should be set against actual RTO

Correctly explains the listener endpoint and DNS re-pointing mechanism
Correctly explains what happens to existing vs. new connections
