questions.title: Diagnosing a Live Blocking Chain Before It Escalates Into a Timeout Storm
questions.prompt: Your monitoring alerts on a spike in query timeouts against a production Azure SQL database. You suspect blocking. Walk through exactly which DMVs you'd query, in what order, to identify the head blocker, confirm what it's actually waiting on (or not waiting on at all), and decide whether to kill it. What's the risk of killing the wrong session?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start with sys.dm_exec_requests filtered to WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0, which immediately shows every currently-blocked session along with the session_id of whatever is blocking it. The goal at this step is to walk the blocking_session_id chain back to its root: if session 80 is blocked by 62, and 62 is itself blocked by 55, then 55 is the actual head blocker -- the one truly-unblocked session everyone downstream is ultimately waiting on, and it's the only one worth investigating further (killing an intermediate blocker like 62 just transfers the block up to whatever 55 is doing, it doesn't resolve anything).

Once I have the head blocker's session_id, I'd check sys.dm_exec_sessions and sys.dm_exec_requests for that specific session: is it actively running a request right now, or does it have an open transaction with no currently-executing request at all (status = 'sleeping' with open_tran_count > 0 in sys.dm_exec_sessions) -- the second case is the much more common and more dangerous pattern: an application opened a transaction, ran some work, and then never committed or rolled back, possibly because the application crashed, hung waiting on a completely separate external call, or a developer forgot a COMMIT on one code path. I'd pull its actual last-run SQL text via sys.dm_exec_sql_text(sql_handle) and check wait_type and wait_resource on sys.dm_exec_requests to see precisely what kind of lock it's sitting on, if anything -- and critically, I'd check whether it's waiting on anything at all, because a head blocker that's simply idle mid-transaction has no wait_type, it's just sitting there holding locks indefinitely.

The risk of killing the wrong session is real and specific: if I kill an intermediate session in the chain rather than the true head blocker, I accomplish nothing -- the block persists because the actual root cause, the head blocker, is untouched, and I've just added a rollback of whatever work that intermediate session was doing to the mess. If I kill the actual head blocker without understanding what it's doing, I force a rollback of its transaction, which could be large (a long-running batch update) and itself take significant time and resources to undo, potentially blocking other things during that rollback, and if it's an application's transaction, I may be forcing an inconsistent partial-completion state the application wasn't built to recover from gracefully. So before killing anything, I want to know roughly how much work the head blocker's transaction has done (to estimate rollback cost) and ideally understand WHY it's stuck open, because sometimes the better fix is addressing the application bug that left the transaction open, not just killing the symptom this one time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I do is hit sys.dm_exec_requests and filter for blocking_session_id not equal to zero -- that gives me the whole picture of who's blocked by whom in one shot. But I don't stop at the first blocker I see; I walk that chain. If A is blocked by B and B is blocked by C, C is the one actually causing all of this, and killing B accomplishes nothing because A would just start waiting on C instead through a different intermediate link.

Once I've got the real head blocker, I want to understand what it's actually doing before I touch it. A lot of the time it's not even running anything right now -- it's sitting there with an open transaction and no active request, which usually means an app opened a transaction, did some work, and just never got around to committing or rolling back, maybe because it crashed or got stuck on something unrelated. I'll pull its last SQL text and check its wait_type to see exactly what lock it's holding and on what resource, if it's even waiting on anything at all.

And I'm genuinely cautious about just killing the head blocker reflexively. If that session has done a lot of work in an open transaction, killing it forces a rollback, and that rollback itself can be slow and resource-intensive -- I could make things worse for a while before they get better. I always want at least a rough sense of what's in that transaction and why it's stuck before I pull the trigger, because the failure mode of killing the wrong session, or killing the right one blindly, is the same mistake in two different flavors: you either don't fix the actual problem, or you create a new, possibly bigger one on top of it.
commonMistakes: Killing the first blocked/blocking session seen without walking the full chain
Assuming the head blocker is always actively running a query rather than idle with an open transaction
Killing a session without estimating rollback cost or understanding what it was doing
Not distinguishing between a session that is waiting on a lock versus one that holds locks while idle
Treating killing the head blocker as a permanent fix rather than addressing the root application cause
keyPoints: sys.dm_exec_requests with blocking_session_id <> 0 reveals the blocking chain
Must walk the chain to the true head blocker, not just the first visible blocking_session_id
Killing an intermediate blocker does not resolve the chain; only the head blocker matters
A head blocker with an open transaction and no active request (sleeping, open_tran_count > 0) is a common, dangerous pattern
Check wait_type/wait_resource and sql_handle text before deciding whether/how to intervene
Killing a session with significant uncommitted work forces a potentially costly rollback

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DMV sequence to identify and walk the blocking chain
Correctly identifies the idle-open-transaction pattern as a common root cause
Correctly uses wait_type/wait_resource/sql_text for diagnosis before acting
Correctly explains the risk of killing the wrong session or killing blindly

questions.title: An Auto-Failover Group Failed Over, But the Application Is Still Down
questions.prompt: An auto-failover group between East US and West US just completed an automatic failover after the primary region had an outage. Monitoring confirms the new primary (former secondary) is up, accepting connections, and healthy. The application is still throwing connection errors 20 minutes later. Walk through the specific, non-obvious reasons this can happen even though the failover itself succeeded, and how you'd check each one.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first and most common cause: the application's connection string isn't pointed at the failover group's listener endpoint at all -- it's hardcoded to the original primary server's own hostname (east-us-primary.database.windows.net instead of sales-fg.database.windows.net). If that's the case, the failover group did exactly what it was supposed to, but the application has no mechanism to discover the new primary at all, because it was never configured to use the thing that actually moves during a failover. I'd check this first by looking at the actual connection string/config the application is using, not assuming it's correct because 'we set up a failover group.'

Second, even when the listener endpoint IS used correctly, DNS TTL and client-side DNS caching can cause a real but bounded delay: the failover group's DNS record has a TTL (commonly short, around 30-60 seconds, by design for exactly this reason), but some clients, OS-level DNS resolvers, or corporate DNS caching layers can hold onto a stale resolution longer than the record's own TTL suggests, especially if a connection pooling layer or a long-lived application process resolved the hostname once at startup and is reusing that cached IP rather than re-resolving per connection. Twenty minutes is longer than I'd expect pure TTL-respecting propagation to take, which points toward either stale caching somewhere in the resolution path, or cause #1 (wrong endpoint entirely) being the actual issue.

Third, firewall rules: if the application's outbound path or the target server's firewall rules were configured only for the old primary's specific scenario (for instance, IP-based firewall rules that were set up assuming traffic patterns relative to the old primary, or if the new primary has different firewall/VNet rule configuration than the old one did -- which can happen if firewall rules weren't provisioned identically on both servers in the pair), the application might be able to resolve to the new primary via DNS but still get rejected at the connection level. I'd check this by looking at connection-level error details specifically (is it a DNS/host-not-found failure, a TCP-level connection refusal, or an actual SQL-level login/firewall rejection) rather than treating all 'connection errors' as the same category.

Fourth, connection pooling on the application side: many connection pool implementations cache open connections and don't necessarily validate/retire them just because DNS now points elsewhere -- if the pool had healthy-looking connections established before the failover (to the now-unreachable or now-secondary old primary) and its validation logic doesn't actively test connections before reuse, it can keep handing out dead or wrong-target connections from the pool well past when fresh connections would have worked, until those pooled connections individually time out and get recycled. I'd check whether an application restart (forcing fresh connections) resolves the issue immediately -- if it does, that strongly points to stale pooled connections rather than anything DNS- or firewall-related.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Since the failover itself clearly worked and the new primary is healthy, I stop thinking about the Azure side and start thinking about everything between the application and that new primary. My first and honestly most common suspicion: is the app actually using the failover group's listener name, or is its connection string hardcoded to the original primary's own server hostname? If it's the latter, this isn't really a failover group problem at all -- the group did its job, the app was just never wired to look at the thing that moves.

If the listener endpoint is configured correctly, next I think about DNS caching. The listener's DNS record has a short TTL specifically so failovers propagate fast, but twenty minutes is longer than I'd expect from TTL alone, which makes me suspicious of something caching more aggressively than it should -- a corporate DNS layer, or more likely, the application resolving the hostname once at startup and holding that IP in memory rather than re-resolving per connection.

I also check the actual error type, because 'connection errors' isn't one thing -- is this DNS failing to resolve, is it a TCP-level refusal, or is it actually reaching a server and getting rejected at the SQL login/firewall layer? That tells me very different things. If it's getting rejected after resolving fine, I'd specifically check whether firewall rules were set up identically on both servers in the pair, because it's easy to configure the primary's firewall carefully and forget the secondary needs the same rules for when it becomes primary.

And finally, I always ask: does restarting the application fix it immediately? If yes, that's a strong signal the real culprit is the connection pool holding onto stale, pre-failover connections that never get revalidated against where DNS now points, and they're just going to keep failing until they individually time out and get replaced — restarting forces that replacement instantly.
commonMistakes: Assuming the failover group itself is broken when the actual issue is application configuration
Treating all connection errors as the same category without checking error type/stage
Assuming DNS propagation alone explains a 20-minute outage without considering caching layers
Forgetting that firewall rules must be configured on both servers in a failover group pair
Not testing whether an application restart resolves the issue to isolate stale connection pooling
keyPoints: Hardcoded connection string to the original server hostname instead of the listener endpoint is the most common root cause
DNS TTL is short by design, but client/OS/application-level caching can exceed it
Connection errors must be categorized (DNS failure vs. TCP refusal vs. SQL-level rejection) to diagnose correctly
Firewall/VNet rules may not be provisioned identically on both servers in the pair
Connection pooling can serve stale pooled connections without re-validating against new DNS resolution
An application restart resolving the issue points strongly to stale pooled connections

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies hardcoded listener-endpoint misconfiguration as a primary suspect
Correctly explains DNS TTL vs. caching behavior as a distinct, bounded cause
Correctly distinguishes error types/stages for diagnosis
Identifies firewall/VNet rule parity between primary and secondary as a cause
Identifies stale connection pooling and the restart test as a diagnostic

questions.title: Troubleshooting Azure SQL Connectivity When the Portal Says Everything Is Healthy
questions.prompt: A new application server, deployed in a VNet-integrated App Service, cannot connect to an Azure SQL Database. The Azure portal shows the database as online and healthy, and the firewall rules look correct at first glance. Walk through the specific, ordered checks you'd run to isolate whether this is a firewall rule, a private endpoint/VNet routing issue, a DNS resolution issue, or an authentication issue -- and explain the one check that distinguishes 'can't reach the server at all' from 'reached the server, got rejected.'
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by establishing which failure mode I'm actually dealing with, because 'cannot connect' from an application log is ambiguous between several very different problems, and most of the time wasted troubleshooting connectivity comes from guessing at the wrong layer. The single most useful check for distinguishing 'can't reach the server at all' from 'reached the server, got rejected' is attempting a raw TCP-level connection test to the server's hostname on port 1433 (or the relevant private endpoint IP), independent of SQL authentication entirely -- using something like Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <server> -Port 1433 from a machine on the same network path as the App Service (or, if VNet-integrated, from a VM in the same VNet/subnet), or tcping/telnet equivalents. If that TCP connection fails outright (times out, connection refused), the problem is at the network/routing/DNS layer, and SQL Server's own login/auth logic was never even reached. If the TCP connection succeeds but the application still fails, the problem is downstream of networking -- most likely authentication, or an application-level connection string issue.

If the TCP test fails, I'd check DNS resolution first and separately from routing: does the hostname resolve to the IP I expect (nslookup/Resolve-DnsName)? For a private-endpoint-connected database, the hostname should resolve to a private IP inside the VNet via the private DNS zone linked to that VNet -- if it's resolving to the database's public IP instead, that tells me the private DNS zone isn't linked to this VNet (or isn't linked correctly), which is one of the most common private endpoint misconfigurations: the private endpoint itself exists and works, but DNS resolution from this specific VNet isn't routing to it. If DNS resolves correctly to the expected (private or public) IP but the TCP connection still fails, I'd check actual routing/NSG rules next -- is there a Network Security Group on the App Service's subnet or the target subnet blocking port 1433 outbound/inbound, and separately, for the public-endpoint case, is the specific firewall rule on the Azure SQL server actually scoped to the right IP (a VNet-integrated App Service without a private endpoint still egresses through a set of outbound IPs that can change, or needs 'Allow Azure services' enabled, which is commonly the actual culprit people overlook when they say 'firewall rules look correct' -- they checked a specific IP rule but the real issue is App Service's outbound IP not matching what they assumed, or needing the VNet integration's own route to a private endpoint rather than relying on IP firewall rules at all).

If the TCP test to port 1433 succeeds, I know the network path is fine and I'd move entirely to the SQL layer: is the actual error a login failure (wrong credential, Entra token issue, or principal lacking access to that specific database), which I'd confirm by trying the exact same credential from SSMS or Azure Data Studio from a machine with equivalent network access, isolating whether it's genuinely an app-specific configuration problem (wrong connection string, wrong managed identity, expired secret) versus something that would fail for any client.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I do, before touching firewall rules or DNS, is separate the question into two completely different problems: can I even reach the server at the network level, or am I reaching it and getting rejected. The one check that answers that cleanly is a raw TCP test to port 1433 -- Test-NetConnection or an equivalent -- run from somewhere on the same network path as the actual failing app, not from my own laptop which might have a totally different route. If that TCP connection doesn't even succeed, this has nothing to do with SQL authentication yet; it's purely networking. If it does succeed, SQL auth and application config become my actual suspects, and I stop looking at firewall/VNet entirely.

If the TCP test fails, I check DNS before anything else, specifically asking whether the hostname is resolving to a private IP or a public one. If this is supposed to go through a private endpoint and it's resolving to the public IP instead, that's almost always a private DNS zone that isn't linked to this particular VNet -- the private endpoint itself can be completely fine and this VNet still can't find it because DNS resolution from here isn't routed to it.

If DNS is resolving correctly but the TCP connection is still failing, I look at NSGs on both the App Service subnet and wherever it's trying to land, and I specifically double-check the 'firewall rules look correct' claim, because that phrase almost always means someone checked an IP allow-list rule and didn't account for 'Allow Azure services' or the fact that a VNet-integrated App Service without a private endpoint egresses through outbound IPs that aren't necessarily what people assumed when they set that rule up.

And if TCP to 1433 succeeds cleanly, I move the whole investigation to the SQL side -- is this a login failure, an Entra token problem, a principal that doesn't have access to this specific database -- and I'd confirm by trying the exact same credential myself from SSMS on a machine with the same network path, to isolate whether it's an app-specific misconfiguration or something that would fail for anyone.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to re-checking firewall IP rules without first isolating network vs. auth layer
Assuming DNS resolving to any IP means resolution is correct, without checking private vs. public
Not checking NSGs on both source and destination subnets
Assuming 'firewall rules look correct' rules out all network-layer causes
Testing from a machine with a different network path than the actual failing application
keyPoints: Raw TCP test to port 1433 (independent of SQL auth) distinguishes network-layer from auth-layer failures
DNS resolution must be checked separately from routing/NSG rules
Private endpoint connectivity requires the private DNS zone to be linked to the specific VNet in question
A VNet-integrated App Service without a private endpoint still egresses via outbound IPs, often missed by IP-based firewall rules
'Allow Azure services' and outbound IP assumptions are common blind spots in 'firewall rules look correct' claims
If TCP succeeds, the investigation should move entirely to authentication/application configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the TCP-level test as the key network/auth distinguishing check
Correctly orders DNS resolution check before routing/NSG checks
Correctly identifies private DNS zone VNet linkage as a common private endpoint failure
Identifies outbound IP/Allow Azure services as a commonly-overlooked firewall gap
Correctly redirects to auth/app-config once network layer is confirmed healthy

questions.title: A Nightly SQL Agent Job Has Been Silently Failing for a Week
questions.prompt: You discover that a nightly SQL Agent job responsible for purging old audit data has failed every night for the past week, but nobody noticed because the failure never triggered an alert. Walk through how you'd investigate what actually went wrong using the job's own history, and then explain the two separate gaps you need to fix: the root cause of the failure itself, and the reason it failed silently for a week without anyone knowing.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the root cause, I'd start in SQL Server Agent's own job history (right-click the job -> View History in SSMS, or query msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory joined to msdb.dbo.sysjobsteps/sysjobs for the full step-level detail) rather than just looking at the job's overall pass/fail status -- the step-level history records which specific step failed and, critically, the actual error message text returned by that step, which is usually enough to point directly at the cause (a permission change, a lock timeout, a referenced object that no longer exists, a full log file, etc.). I'd pull history for all seven failed runs, not just the most recent one, specifically to check whether the error is identical every night (pointing to a single persistent cause, like a schema change or revoked permission) or whether it varies night to night (pointing to something more transient/environmental, like resource contention with another overlapping job, or growing data volume causing a timeout that didn't occur when the table was smaller).

Once I have the actual error text, I'd reproduce the underlying command manually in a query window under the same security context the job step runs as (jobs often run as a specific proxy account or under the SQL Server Agent service account, not as me) to confirm the exact failure and test a fix before re-enabling the schedule.

There are genuinely two separate problems here, and fixing only the first one means this happens again with some other failure later. The first is the root cause of this specific failure -- whatever the error message points to. The second, and the one that actually matters more for preventing a repeat of 'nobody noticed for a week,' is why failure didn't trigger any notification. That's almost always one of: no operator/alert was ever configured on the job step at all (the job step's 'On Failure' action needs to be explicitly set to notify an operator, it's not automatic just because the job exists); an operator was configured but its notification method (email, in this case) was pointed at an address nobody monitors, or Database Mail itself was misconfigured/broken so the notification was generated internally but never actually delivered; or the job's own failure didn't propagate an alert because the alert definition (via sp_add_alert) that should fire on SQL Server Agent job failure for this specific job either doesn't exist or is scoped incorrectly. I'd check each of these in order -- job step properties for the on-failure notification setting, the operator's configured email and whether Database Mail logs show successful or failed delivery attempts, and whether a matching alert exists at all -- because silently-failing automation is, from a DBA process standpoint, often a bigger risk than the original bug, since it means the team has no visibility into failures by design, not by bad luck this one time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd go straight to the job's history, but at the step level, not just the overall job status -- that's where the real error message lives, in sysjobhistory joined with the job and step tables, or just View History in SSMS. I pull all seven nights of failures, not just last night's, specifically because I want to know if it's the exact same error every time or something that's drifting -- that tells me whether I'm looking at one fixed root cause or something more environmental, like contention with another job or a growing table starting to time out.

Once I've got the actual error text, I try to reproduce it myself, running the same command manually under whatever security context the job actually runs as, because jobs often run as a proxy account, not as me, and testing under my own permissions can give a false 'it works fine' result that doesn't match what's actually happening at 2 a.m.

But I'm always careful to treat this as two separate bugs, not one. There's the actual root cause of the purge job failing, and then there's the much more important question of why nobody got paged about it for seven nights straight. That second one is usually one of three things: the job step was never configured to notify anyone on failure in the first place, an operator exists but their email isn't actually monitored or Database Mail itself is silently broken so nothing ever got delivered, or there's just no alert wired up at all for this job's failure. I check all three, because fixing the purge script but leaving the alerting gap means we're exactly one different bug away from this happening again, and next time it might not be something as low-stakes as an audit purge.
commonMistakes: Looking only at the overall job status rather than step-level error detail
Only investigating the most recent failure instead of comparing the full week's pattern
Testing the fix under the DBA's own permissions instead of the job's actual execution context
Fixing the root cause but not investigating why no alert fired
Assuming an operator being configured means notifications are actually being delivered
keyPoints: Step-level job history (sysjobhistory/sysjobsteps) reveals the actual error message, not just pass/fail status
Comparing all failed runs, not just the latest, distinguishes a fixed cause from a drifting/environmental one
Reproducing the failing command under the job's actual execution security context, not the DBA's own
Root cause and alerting-gap are two separate problems that both need fixing
Alerting gaps are typically: missing on-failure notification config, broken/misdirected Database Mail, or missing alert definition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes using step-level job history to find the root cause
Correctly reasons about comparing multiple failed runs for pattern
Correctly emphasizes reproducing under the job's actual security context
Clearly separates root cause from the alerting/notification gap
Correctly enumerates realistic reasons the failure alert never fired

questions.title: DBCC CHECKDB Reports Corruption in a Production Database — What You Do in the Next Ten Minutes
questions.prompt: A scheduled DBCC CHECKDB run against a production database reports consistency errors overnight. Walk through exactly what you do first, before attempting any repair, and explain specifically why running DBCC CHECKDB WITH REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS immediately is almost always the wrong first move even though it's the option that sounds most thorough.
questions.modelAnswer:
The very first thing I do is NOT touch the database with any repair option -- I read the actual CHECKDB output in full, because the specific errors reported determine everything downstream, and I need to know the scope (how many objects/pages affected, whether it's isolated to one nonclustered index, one table, or something in a system table/allocation structure) before deciding anything. I'd specifically check whether the corruption is confined to a nonclustered index -- if so, this is usually the best-case scenario, because a nonclustered index can be safely dropped and rebuilt from the clustered index/heap data without any data loss and without needing REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS at all, since the index itself contains no data that doesn't exist elsewhere.

Second, I verify exactly what backups exist and their recency and integrity -- when was the last full backup, are there log backups since then giving me point-in-time recovery options, and have those backups themselves ever been tested with a restore (corruption that's gone undetected for a while can mean several backup generations already contain the same corrupted pages, which is exactly why regular CHECKDB runs and backup verification both matter). This determines my actual options: if I have a clean backup from before the corruption started and point-in-time log backups to roll forward to just before the issue, a restore is almost always safer and more complete than any in-place repair.

Third, I isolate the root cause, or at least rule out an active one: is this corruption from a one-time event (an unexpected shutdown, a storage-level glitch) or is there an ongoing hardware/storage problem that will just corrupt things again right after I fix them? I'd check the Windows/storage event logs for disk errors around the time the corruption likely started, because repairing or restoring without addressing an active storage problem just buys time until it recurs.

The reason REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS as an immediate first move is almost always wrong, despite sounding thorough, is in its own name: it is explicitly allowed to delete data to get the database back to a structurally consistent state. It doesn't recover or reconstruct the corrupted data -- for corruption in a data page, its typical action is literally deallocating and removing the corrupted page and whatever rows lived on it, which is real, permanent, irreversible data loss, chosen specifically because Microsoft's own guidance treats it as a last resort when there is no viable backup, not a routine first response. Running it before even reading the scope of damage or checking backup options means potentially discarding recoverable data in a one-step, un-undoable operation, for problems that a nonclustered index rebuild or a restore-and-roll-forward could have fixed with zero data loss. It's also run in single-user mode, meaning it requires taking the database offline to every other user during the operation -- a disruptive step you don't want to take before you've even confirmed it's the right tool.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The very first thing I do is nothing destructive -- I sit down and actually read the full CHECKDB output, because the specific errors tell me the scope, and scope changes everything about what the right next move is. If this is corruption confined to a nonclustered index, I'm actually relieved, because that's the easy case -- I can just drop and rebuild that index from the underlying clustered data, no data loss, no REPAIR option needed at all.

At the same time, I'm checking exactly what backups I have -- how recent is the last full backup, do I have log backups since then that would let me restore and roll forward to right before this happened, and honestly, have those backups ever actually been test-restored, because it's entirely possible this corruption has been sitting undetected for a while and several backup generations already have it baked in.

I also want to rule out whether this was a one-time blip or an ongoing storage problem, because fixing the database and having the same hardware issue corrupt it again a day later isn't actually fixing anything -- I'd check the server's disk/event logs around when this likely started.

And I'd specifically push back on reaching for REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS right away, even though the name makes it sound like the comprehensive option. It's the opposite of comprehensive -- its actual mechanism for fixing a corrupted data page is usually to just deallocate that page and the rows on it, which is permanent data loss, by design, and it puts the database in single-user mode to do it. Microsoft is explicit that this is meant to be a last resort when you genuinely have no usable backup, not a default first response, and running it before I've even confirmed backup options or the real scope of the damage means I might be throwing away recoverable data for a problem a restore or an index rebuild would have fixed cleanly.
commonMistakes: Running REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS immediately without reading the full error scope first
Assuming all corruption requires the same repair approach regardless of what structure is affected
Not checking whether existing backups predate the corruption or already contain it
Repairing without investigating whether an active storage/hardware issue will cause recurrence
Treating REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS as data recovery rather than understanding it discards data
keyPoints: Read full CHECKDB output first to determine scope before any repair action
Corruption confined to a nonclustered index can be fixed by drop/rebuild with zero data loss
Verify backup recency, point-in-time log backup chain, and whether backups have been tested
Check for an ongoing storage/hardware root cause before repairing, to avoid immediate recurrence
REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS typically deallocates corrupted pages/rows as its actual fix mechanism
REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS requires single-user mode and is a documented last resort, not a first move

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes reading full CHECKDB output/scope before acting
Correctly identifies nonclustered index corruption as a zero-data-loss case
Correctly prioritizes backup verification and restore options
Checks for an ongoing root cause to avoid recurrence
Correctly explains why REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS is a last resort, with accurate mechanism

questions.title: A Query Regressed Right After an Index Change — Using Query Store to Confirm and Roll Back
questions.prompt: A developer rebuilt an index differently last Tuesday to 'optimize' a report. Since then, a previously fast query has become unpredictably slow, sometimes fast, sometimes taking 20x longer with no code change. Using Query Store, explain exactly how you'd confirm the index change is the actual cause rather than coincidence, and why this specific symptom pattern (inconsistent, not uniformly slow) points to plan instability rather than a simple missing index.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start in Query Store's plan history for this specific query (via sys.query_store_plan joined to sys.query_store_query, filtered by the query text/query_id) and look at the full timeline of distinct plan_ids used for that query, ordered by their first-seen time. If a new plan_id appears starting right around last Tuesday, that's direct, specific evidence correlating a plan change in time with the index rebuild -- not just a plausible story, but something I can point to with an actual timestamp and plan_id, which I'd then compare using Query Store's 'Compare Plans' view (or querying sys.query_store_runtime_stats per plan_id) to see the old plan's historical average duration/logical reads versus the new plan's.

The inconsistent symptom -- sometimes fast, sometimes 20x slower, with no code change -- is itself diagnostic, and it's specifically NOT what a simple 'missing index now causing a scan' problem looks like: a missing index produces a plan that's uniformly bad every single time the query runs, because the optimizer picks the same (now-worse) plan consistently given the same statistics and schema. Inconsistency between executions instead points toward parameter sniffing / plan instability: the query likely has a parameterized or templated WHERE clause, and the specific parameter value used on the FIRST execution after a plan was evicted from cache (or after the index rebuild invalidated/recompiled the plan) gets compiled into a plan optimized for that specific value's estimated selectivity -- if that first value happened to be a rare value, the optimizer might choose a seek-heavy plan assuming few rows; if the next first-after-recompile value is actually common, that same cached plan now processes far more rows than it was shaped for, running dramatically slower, until the plan gets evicted/recompiled again and the cycle repeats with a different parameter value. The index rebuild didn't necessarily make the underlying index worse -- it very plausibly reset statistics or forced a recompile at a moment when an atypical parameter value got baked into the next cached plan, and the real issue is that the query's plan is sensitive to parameter value in a way that isn't being handled (missing OPTION (RECOMPILE) where appropriate, missing OPTIMIZE FOR hints, or the query needing to be restructured to avoid a single one-size-fits-all plan for a skewed data distribution).

To confirm this specifically, I'd look at Query Store's runtime stats for the SAME plan_id across multiple executions and check for high variance in duration/logical reads within that one plan, rather than consistent values -- high variance within a single plan_id is a strong additional signal of parameter-sensitive plan reuse, separate from the plan-change evidence. Once confirmed, the fix isn't necessarily 'undo the index rebuild' at all (the index might even be fine) -- it's addressing the parameter sensitivity directly, and in the meantime, forcing a known-stable plan via sp_query_store_force_plan is the fast mitigation while a real fix (recompile hints, query restructuring) is worked out.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First move is Query Store's plan history for this exact query -- I want to see every distinct plan_id it's used and when each one first showed up. If a brand new plan appears right around last Tuesday, that's not a coincidence I'm guessing at, that's a timestamp I can point to directly tying the plan change to the index rebuild. From there I'd pull runtime stats for the old plan versus the new one and compare average duration and reads directly.

But the specific symptom here — sometimes fast, sometimes dramatically slower, same query, same code — is actually more interesting to me than just 'the new index made it worse,' because a genuinely bad or missing index produces consistently bad performance every time, not a coin flip. Inconsistency like this is the classic signature of parameter sniffing. What probably happened is the index rebuild forced a recompile, and whatever specific value happened to run first after that recompile got baked into the cached plan based on its own selectivity — if that value was rare, SQL Server built a plan assuming very few matching rows, and that plan gets reused for every subsequent call until it's evicted again, even when a totally different, much more common value comes through and that same narrow plan ends up processing way more data than it was shaped for.

To actually confirm that's what's happening rather than just theorize it, I'd look inside Query Store at the runtime stats for a single plan_id across its many executions and check whether duration is wildly inconsistent even within that one plan — if it is, that's strong evidence of parameter-sensitive reuse, on top of the timing correlation with the index change. And the fix, once I've confirmed this, usually isn't 'revert the index' at all — the index might be totally fine — it's addressing the parameter sensitivity itself, maybe with a recompile hint or restructuring the query, while using sp_query_store_force_plan on a known-stable plan as the immediate band-aid.
commonMistakes: Assuming any post-change slowdown is automatically caused by the index change without timeline correlation
Treating inconsistent performance the same as uniformly bad performance diagnostically
Jumping to 'revert the index' without confirming the actual mechanism (parameter sniffing)
Not checking variance within a single plan_id's own runtime stats
Forgetting sp_query_store_force_plan as an immediate mitigation while root-causing
keyPoints: Query Store plan history timeline correlates a new plan_id's appearance with the index rebuild timestamp
Comparing runtime stats per plan_id confirms whether the new plan is actually worse on average
Inconsistent (not uniformly bad) performance is the signature of parameter sniffing/plan instability, not a simple missing-index regression
A missing/degraded index produces consistently bad performance, not variable performance
High variance in runtime stats within a single plan_id is corroborating evidence of parameter-sensitive reuse
The fix is addressing parameter sensitivity (recompile hints, restructuring), not necessarily reverting the index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses Query Store plan history to correlate timing with the index change
Correctly explains why inconsistent performance indicates parameter sniffing, not a simple missing index
Correctly uses within-plan runtime stats variance as corroborating evidence
Proposes a correct fix approach (recompile hints/restructuring) rather than reflexively reverting the index

questions.title: Troubleshooting a Login That Works in SSMS But Fails From the Application
questions.prompt: A service account can connect to Azure SQL Database fine from SSMS on your machine, but the production application using the exact same login fails with a permission error on one specific stored procedure call. Walk through the specific, non-obvious reasons this happens even though 'it's the same login,' and how you'd isolate which one applies here.
questions.modelAnswer:
The phrase 'exact same login' hides several differences that commonly explain this exact symptom. First, and most common: the application and SSMS may be connecting to different databases entirely, or the same database but the login's associated database user has different permissions than expected in that specific database context -- a login can exist at the server level but have a contained database user mapped in one database with certain role memberships, and no mapping (or different role memberships) in another database the application actually targets. I'd check this first by confirming, from the application's own connection string, the exact database (and server, if there's any chance of a failover group or multiple environments) it's connecting to, not assuming it matches what I tested in SSMS.

Second, execution context inside the stored procedure itself: if the procedure references objects in another database or schema, or calls EXECUTE AS within its own definition, or the procedure was created with a specific owner whose permissions are what actually matter (ownership chaining) rather than the calling login's direct permissions, the calling login's own grants might be irrelevant to whether the proc succeeds -- what matters is whether the chain of ownership/execution context resolves permissions the way everyone assumes. I'd check the procedure's actual definition for EXECUTE AS, cross-database/cross-schema references, and ownership, since 'permission error on one specific procedure' (not a broad permission failure) often points to something specific to that one object's definition rather than a login-wide problem.

Third, and specifically relevant for Azure SQL with Entra authentication: if the application authenticates via a managed identity or an Entra service principal rather than literally the same SQL login credential I used in SSMS, 'same login' might not be as literal as it sounds -- a managed identity resolves to its own distinct database principal with its own grants, separate from a human Entra account or SQL login that happens to share a similar-sounding name, and I'd explicitly verify, via sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members, which actual principal the application's connection maps to versus which principal my SSMS session maps to -- they may not be the identical principal at all despite both being described informally as 'the service account.'

Fourth, parameter/context differences: if the stored procedure's logic branches based on something like SUSER_NAME(), ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), or application-supplied parameters that differ between my manual SSMS test and what the real application actually passes, the procedure could be failing a permission check inside its own logic (not a SQL-engine-level GRANT/DENY) that only triggers for certain input -- so I'd also compare whether I'm calling the procedure with genuinely identical parameters, not just 'as the same login.'

To isolate which applies, I'd: confirm the exact database/server the application targets and reconnect SSMS to that exact same target; query sys.database_principals / sys.database_role_members for both my SSMS session's actual resolved principal and (via application logging or a DBA trace) the application's actual resolved principal, to confirm they're truly identical; and inspect the procedure's definition for EXECUTE AS/ownership chaining/cross-database references before assuming the problem is login-level permissions at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The phrase that always makes me suspicious here is 'exact same login' — in practice that phrase hides a lot of ways things can actually be different. My first check is whether the application is even connecting to the same database I tested in SSMS — a login can have completely different permissions depending on which database's user mapping actually applies, and it's easy to test in SSMS against one environment while the app is quietly pointed at another.

If the database genuinely matches, I go look at the stored procedure's own definition next, because a failure on one specific procedure rather than a broad permission error usually means something about that procedure itself, not the login overall. Does it use EXECUTE AS inside its body? Does it reference objects in another schema or database? Ownership chaining means the permissions that actually matter for that cross-reference might belong to the procedure's owner, not to whoever's calling it — so the calling login's own grants can be completely beside the point.

In Azure SQL specifically, I also ask whether the application is actually authenticating the same way I am. If it's using a managed identity or a service principal and I tested with a SQL login or my own Entra account, those are genuinely different principals under the hood even if everyone's been casually calling both of them 'the service account' — I'd go check sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members for both and confirm they're actually the same object, not just similarly named.

And finally, I check whether the procedure's logic itself branches on something like the caller's identity or specific parameter values — because if it does, this might not be a GRANT/DENY problem at the engine level at all, it might be the procedure's own internal logic rejecting a specific input the app happens to send that I never tested manually. I'd walk through all four of these in order rather than assuming the first plausible one is the real answer.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'same login name' guarantees identical effective permissions across databases
Not checking the stored procedure's definition for EXECUTE AS or ownership chaining
Assuming a managed identity and a similarly-named SQL login are the same underlying principal
Testing with different parameters than the application actually sends and assuming that's equivalent
Jumping to re-granting broad permissions without isolating the actual cause first
keyPoints: Login/user mapping can differ by database — confirm the application targets the exact same database
Ownership chaining/EXECUTE AS inside the procedure can make the owner's permissions, not the caller's, the deciding factor
Managed identity/service principal authentication resolves to a distinct principal from a human/Entra account with a similar name
sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members should be used to confirm both sessions resolve to the truly identical principal
The procedure's own internal logic (not just GRANT/DENY) can reject specific parameter values or identities

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies database-specific user mapping as a candidate cause
Correctly explains ownership chaining/EXECUTE AS as a procedure-specific cause
Correctly distinguishes managed identity/service principal from a similarly-named login
Identifies procedure-internal logic/parameter differences as a possible cause
Describes a sound isolation method (sys.database_principals, role_members, proc definition)

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario

Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Designing an Always On Availability Group Topology for a Multi-Region DR Requirement
questions.prompt: A client runs SQL Server on Azure VMs (not Azure SQL Database) for a legacy application that can't move to PaaS yet. They need: zero data loss for a same-datacenter server failure, and survival of an entire region outage with an acceptable, pre-agreed small amount of data loss. Design the Always On Availability Group topology — replica count, synchronous vs. asynchronous commit per replica, and automatic vs. manual failover per replica — that satisfies both requirements, and explain why a single topology can satisfy both.
questions.modelAnswer:
This requires at least three replicas across two distinct failure domains: two replicas in the primary region (the current primary plus at least one secondary, both configured for synchronous commit with automatic failover between them), and a third replica in a secondary Azure region configured for asynchronous commit with manual failover only.

The two same-region replicas satisfy the first requirement directly: synchronous commit means a transaction isn't acknowledged as committed to the client until it's hardened on both the primary and the synchronous secondary, so a failure of the primary server alone (not the whole datacenter/region) loses zero committed transactions — the secondary already has everything, and automatic failover (requiring a third quorum-contributing element, typically a file share witness or the cluster's own quorum mechanism, since Windows Server Failover Clustering needs quorum to safely automate failover decisions) can promote it without a human needing to intervene, usually within seconds.

The cross-region replica satisfies the second requirement specifically because it is NOT synchronous — synchronous commit across regions would mean every transaction waits on a round-trip to a different Azure region before being acknowledged, which adds real, likely unacceptable latency to every single write for a workload that otherwise doesn't need it; asynchronous commit lets the primary acknowledge transactions locally and ship them to the cross-region replica without blocking on it, which is exactly why cross-region HA/DR setups accept a small RPO rather than zero — there's always some number of transactions in flight that haven't yet reached the async replica when a true regional disaster strikes. Manual failover (rather than automatic) is deliberately chosen for the cross-region replica because a region-wide outage is a major, consequential event that should involve a human decision (confirming the primary region is actually down, not just experiencing a transient network partition that would make failing over unnecessary and disruptive) and because the automatic-failover quorum mechanics that work cleanly within one region's low-latency network don't translate safely to blindly automating a decision across regions with higher, variable latency.

One topology satisfies both requirements because the two concerns are decomposed onto different replicas with different settings rather than forcing one blended compromise: the in-region pair is tuned entirely for the zero-data-loss, fast-automatic-failover requirement, and the cross-region replica is tuned entirely for the 'survive losing an entire region, with an accepted small RPO' requirement, and Always On Availability Groups explicitly support mixing synchronous and asynchronous replicas with different failover modes within the same group, rather than requiring every replica to share one policy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this as three replicas, not two, because the two requirements genuinely need different replication behavior and trying to satisfy both with one setting would mean compromising on one of them. In the primary region, I'd put the current primary and one synchronous secondary, with automatic failover between the two — synchronous commit means a transaction isn't considered done until both copies have it, so losing just the primary server doesn't lose any committed data, and automatic failover through the cluster's quorum mechanism means that happens without anyone picking up a phone.

Then a third replica goes in a different Azure region entirely, and that one is asynchronous with manual failover, very deliberately. Asynchronous because making every write wait on a round-trip to another region would tank write performance for a workload that doesn't otherwise need that latency — so I'm trading a small, agreed amount of possible data loss for keeping normal operations fast. Manual failover because a whole-region outage is the kind of event I actually want a human eyeballing before triggering — confirming this is real and not some transient blip — and automated quorum-based failover decisions that work great within one low-latency region don't translate cleanly across a higher-latency, cross-region link.

The reason one topology handles both requirements is that I'm not trying to force one replication setting to do two jobs — I'm assigning each requirement to the replica pair that's actually suited for it. Always On is explicitly built to let you mix sync and async replicas with different failover modes in the same availability group, so this isn't a workaround, it's exactly the intended use of the feature for this kind of layered HA/DR requirement.
commonMistakes: Using synchronous commit across regions, adding unacceptable write latency
Using automatic failover for the cross-region replica without accounting for quorum/latency risk
Assuming two replicas (one sync, one async) is sufficient without a true in-region automatic-failover pair
Believing a single availability group can't mix synchronous and asynchronous replica settings
Not recognizing that zero-RPO and regional survival are two separate requirements needing separate replica settings
keyPoints: Three replicas: two same-region (synchronous, automatic failover), one cross-region (asynchronous, manual failover)
Synchronous commit guarantees zero data loss for a same-region server-level failure
Automatic failover requires quorum, which is reliable within a single low-latency region
Asynchronous commit across regions avoids adding cross-region latency to every write
Manual failover for the cross-region replica reflects the judgment call a regional disaster requires
Always On supports mixing sync/async and automatic/manual settings within a single availability group

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the three-replica topology with appropriate commit modes
Correctly explains why synchronous commit satisfies the zero-data-loss same-region requirement
Correctly explains why asynchronous commit is required cross-region and its RPO implication
Correctly justifies manual failover for the cross-region replica
Explains why one topology can satisfy both requirements via decomposition

questions.title: Auto-Failover Groups vs. Active Geo-Replication: Choosing the Right Tool
questions.prompt: A client has 40 databases on a single Azure SQL logical server and wants disaster recovery to a secondary region. Another team in the same company runs 3 critical databases that each need independent, fine-grained control over which specific secondary region they replicate to, with different failover timing for each database. Design the DR approach for each team and justify why auto-failover groups suit one and active geo-replication suits the other, including what you'd lose by using the wrong one for each case.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the first team's 40 databases on one logical server, an auto-failover group is the correct fit specifically because it operates at the server level: you configure the group once, between the primary server and a single secondary server, and every database on that server (current and future, since failover groups can be configured to include all databases on the server automatically) replicates and fails over together, as a single unit, through one stable listener endpoint. This is exactly the right shape for '40 databases that should all move to the same secondary region together, consistently, without needing per-database configuration' — it dramatically reduces operational overhead versus configuring and monitoring 40 separate replication relationships, and automatic failover with a single grace period policy applies uniformly.

For the second team's 3 databases, active geo-replication (configured per-database, outside the failover-group construct) is the correct fit specifically because it allows each database to have its own independent secondary — potentially in different regions from each other — and its own readable secondary count/configuration, without being tied to what any other database (on the same or a different server) is doing. Active geo-replication also, notably, supports up to four secondaries per database (useful for read-scale fanout in addition to DR) versus a failover group's simpler primary/secondary-pair shape, and because it's configured per database, failover timing and the decision to fail over can genuinely be made independently per database rather than as an all-or-nothing group action.

What you'd lose using the wrong one for each case: if the 40-database team used active geo-replication instead of a failover group, they'd have to configure and separately monitor 40 individual replication relationships, there'd be no single listener endpoint abstracting 'where the primary currently is' for application connection strings (each database's own endpoint would need separate handling), and failing over 40 databases consistently together during a real incident would require either careful manual orchestration or custom automation that a failover group gives you for free. If the 3-critical-database team used a single auto-failover group instead, they'd be forced into one shared secondary server/region for all three and one shared failover policy/grace period, losing the ability to send one database to a different region than another or to fail over one independently without affecting the other two — exactly the fine-grained, independent control their requirement explicitly calls for.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the 40-database team, I'm reaching straight for an auto-failover group, because it's built exactly for this shape of problem — it operates at the server level, so I configure the relationship once between the primary and secondary server, and every database on that server rides along as a unit through one listener endpoint. Trying to manage 40 individual geo-replication relationships instead would mean 40 things to configure, 40 things to monitor, and no single abstraction for 'where is the primary right now' that the application layer can just point at.

For the 3 critical databases that each need to go to potentially different regions with independently-controlled failover timing, that's precisely where a failover group stops being the right tool, because a group ties everything on that server to one shared secondary and one shared failover policy. Active geo-replication configured per database is what gives this team the actual independence they're asking for — each database can have its own secondary region, its own readable-secondary setup, even up to four secondaries if they wanted read-scale on top of DR, and failing one over doesn't force the other two to move with it.

If I swapped these — forced the 40-database team onto individual geo-replication, or crammed the 3 independent-requirement databases into one shared failover group — I'd be creating exactly the problem each team is trying to avoid. The 40-database team would lose the operational simplicity that's the whole point of using a group at that scale, and the 3-database team would lose the per-database regional and timing independence that's explicitly their actual requirement, forcing all three onto one secondary region and one failover decision whether they like it or not.
commonMistakes: Assuming active geo-replication and failover groups are interchangeable regardless of scale or independence needs
Forcing many databases into separate geo-replication relationships instead of one failover group
Forcing databases that need independent regions/timing into one shared failover group
Forgetting that failover groups provide a listener endpoint that per-database geo-replication does not
Not recognizing active geo-replication's multi-secondary (up to 4) read-scale capability
keyPoints: Auto-failover groups operate at the server level, covering all (or all-configured) databases as a single unit
Active geo-replication is configured per database, allowing independent secondary regions and timing
Failover groups provide one stable listener endpoint, simplifying application connection strings at scale
Active geo-replication supports up to four secondaries per database, useful for read-scale beyond just DR
Using a failover group for databases needing independent regions/timing forces them into one shared policy
Using per-database geo-replication for a large uniform fleet multiplies operational/monitoring overhead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends failover group for the 40-database uniform fleet with justification
Correctly recommends active geo-replication for the 3 independent databases with justification
Correctly explains server-level vs. per-database scope distinction
Correctly explains the operational cost of choosing the wrong tool in each case
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Choosing Between Provisioned vCore, Serverless, and Hyperscale for Three Different Workloads
questions.prompt: You're advising on compute tier selection for three Azure SQL Database workloads: (1) a steady, 24/7 high-throughput OLTP system with predictable load, (2) an internal reporting database used in bursts during business hours on weekdays only, largely idle overnight and weekends, and (3) a rapidly-growing database currently at 800GB that's expected to reach several terabytes within a year and occasionally needs near-instant restores for testing. Recommend a tier for each and justify why the other two tiers would be a worse fit for that specific workload.
questions.modelAnswer:
For workload (1), the steady 24/7 high-throughput OLTP system, provisioned vCore (General Purpose, or Business Critical if latency/IO characteristics demand it) is the right fit: provisioned compute means a fixed, dedicated amount of vCores and memory are allocated continuously, which is exactly aligned with a workload that's actually using capacity nearly all the time — you're paying a predictable rate for capacity you're genuinely consuming around the clock. Serverless would be a poor fit here because its value proposition is auto-pausing and auto-scaling during idle/variable periods — for a workload with no idle periods to speak of, serverless's auto-scale overhead (and its per-second compute billing model, which is specifically designed to save money by scaling DOWN during idle time) provides no benefit and can actually cost more than provisioned pricing for sustained, predictable high usage, since serverless's pricing model is built around variability, not steady saturation. Hyperscale would also be a worse fit unless this workload also has unusual storage-scale or backup/restore-speed needs — Hyperscale's real differentiator is its distributed storage architecture, which matters most when storage size or backup/restore speed is the actual bottleneck, not raw sustained compute throughput, so choosing it here would add complexity without addressing this workload's actual characteristic.

For workload (2), the business-hours-only reporting database, serverless is the right fit precisely because its core mechanism — auto-pausing compute during sustained inactivity and auto-scaling vCores within a configured min/max range based on actual load — directly matches a workload that's predictably idle for large stretches (nights, weekends) and only needs real compute during business hours. Billing based on vCores actually used per second, plus near-zero cost during the paused state, means you're not paying full provisioned rate for capacity sitting unused the majority of the week. Provisioned vCore would be a worse fit because you'd be paying for the same fixed capacity 24/7 regardless of the fact that most of that time, little or nothing is happening — you'd be funding idle compute most of the week. Hyperscale isn't the right lens for this decision at all, since the deciding factor here is compute utilization pattern, not storage scale.

For workload (3), the rapidly-growing multi-terabyte database needing fast restores for testing, Hyperscale is the right fit precisely because of its distributed, page-server storage architecture: it scales storage independently of compute, into many terabytes, without the downtime a storage resize forces on General Purpose/Business Critical, and its backup/restore mechanism is near-instant snapshot-based rather than a traditional backup job whose duration scales with database size — which directly addresses 'occasionally needs near-instant restores for testing' in a way neither other tier can match (a multi-terabyte database's restore time on General Purpose/Business Critical scales up substantially with size, which is precisely the problem Hyperscale's architecture was built to solve). Provisioned vCore (General Purpose/Business Critical) would be a worse fit as the database grows, both because of the eventual storage ceiling and because restore times would keep getting worse as the database grows toward multiple terabytes. Serverless would be a particularly poor fit here, since serverless is about compute elasticity for variable load, and says nothing about solving the storage-scale or restore-speed problem this workload actually has — picking it would mean solving the wrong axis of the problem entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the steady 24/7 OLTP system, I'd go provisioned vCore without much hesitation — that workload is using real capacity basically all the time, so a fixed, dedicated allocation at a predictable rate is exactly what matches it. Serverless would be solving a problem this workload doesn't have — there's no meaningful idle time for auto-pause or auto-scale to actually save money on, and Hyperscale's whole value is around storage architecture, which isn't really this workload's bottleneck unless there's something else going on with its data size.

For the business-hours-only reporting database, that's almost a textbook serverless case — it's predictably idle most of the week, and serverless auto-pauses during that idle time and auto-scales up for the bursts during business hours, so I'm not paying a full provisioned rate around the clock for capacity that's mostly sitting there doing nothing nights and weekends. Provisioned vCore would mean paying full price for all that unused time, which is exactly the cost serverless exists to avoid.

And for the rapidly-growing, multi-terabyte database that needs fast test restores, Hyperscale is the one actual fit here, because the real problem isn't compute at all — it's storage scale and restore speed, and that's specifically what Hyperscale's distributed storage architecture was built to solve, with near-instant snapshot-based restores regardless of size and storage scaling that doesn't force downtime the way a resize would on the other tiers. Provisioned vCore would just get slower to restore and more constrained as this thing grows toward multiple terabytes, and serverless doesn't even address the actual bottleneck — it's solving a compute-elasticity problem for a workload whose real issue is storage and restore speed.
commonMistakes: Recommending serverless for a steady, always-busy workload
Recommending provisioned vCore for a predictably idle, bursty workload without considering serverless cost savings
Recommending Hyperscale based on raw throughput needs rather than storage scale/restore-speed needs
Assuming Hyperscale is simply 'a bigger vCore tier' rather than a different storage architecture
Not addressing why the other two tiers are specifically worse for each workload, only naming one tier per case
keyPoints: Provisioned vCore fits steady, continuously-high-utilization workloads at a predictable rate
Serverless auto-pauses/auto-scales compute, fitting workloads with predictable idle periods
Hyperscale's differentiator is distributed storage, delivering fast restores independent of database size
Serverless provides no benefit (and can cost more) for workloads with no real idle time
Provisioned tiers' restore time scales with database size, unlike Hyperscale's snapshot-based restores
Matching the tier to the workload's actual bottleneck (compute utilization pattern vs. storage scale) is the deciding factor
