questions.title: Designing the Monitoring-to-Automation Feedback Loop for Fleet-Wide Index Health
questions.prompt: Tie together Query Store, Automatic Tuning, and Elastic Jobs into a single coherent architecture that keeps index health reasonable across a 150-database fleet with minimal manual intervention, while leaving a clear, documented path for a DBA to intervene when automation isn't enough. Explain how these three pieces hand off to each other rather than operating as three unrelated tools someone happened to enable.
questions.modelAnswer:
The three pieces form a layered pipeline where each one's output is the next one's input, rather than three independent, unrelated systems:

Query Store is the foundation layer -- enabled fleet-wide, it continuously captures query text, plan, and runtime statistics per database, and this captured data is what both of the other two systems depend on entirely; without Query Store enabled and properly retained, Automatic Tuning has no regression history to detect against, and any Elastic Job logic that queries fragmentation/usage stats for decision-making is working with less complete information about actual query impact.

Automatic Tuning sits on top of Query Store as the first line of automated response, specifically for plan regressions (FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN automatically reverting a query to a previously-good plan when Query Store's own data shows a regression) -- this handles the most common, lowest-judgment-required class of index/plan health issue without any human or scheduled job involved at all, reacting essentially in near-real-time as regressions are detected.

Elastic Jobs is the scheduled, fleet-wide orchestration layer that handles the maintenance Automatic Tuning doesn't cover on its own: periodic index fragmentation checks and rebuild/reorganize operations (which Automatic Tuning's plan-forcing doesn't address at all -- a fragmented index can still get a 'good' plan forced onto it that's simply operating on degraded physical structure), and critically, a scheduled job that specifically surfaces Automatic Tuning's own recommendation/action HISTORY across the fleet into one consolidated report (querying sys.dm_db_tuning_recommendations or the Automatic Tuning history views on each database via the target-group mechanism) rather than requiring a DBA to check each of 150 databases' tuning history individually.

The documented manual-intervention path sits explicitly on top of this pipeline, not disconnected from it: the Elastic Job's consolidated weekly report is the DBA's actual entry point -- it flags databases where Automatic Tuning fired unusually often (suggesting a deeper, recurring issue being band-aided rather than fixed), index recommendations that were surfaced but not auto-applied (left deliberately for human judgment because of their consequence level), and fragmentation levels that keep recurring quickly after a rebuild (suggesting a workload/fill-factor mismatch Automatic Tuning and routine rebuilds won't resolve on their own). This report becomes the DBA's prioritized worklist rather than them needing to proactively hunt for problems across 150 databases -- the automation handles the routine, high-volume, low-judgment cases entirely on its own, and specifically surfaces, rather than silently swallows, the cases that actually need a human's judgment, which is the whole point of designing the handoff deliberately rather than just turning three separate features on and hoping they overlap usefully.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I think about this as a pipeline where each layer feeds the next, not three separate features someone flipped on independently. Query Store is the foundation — it's capturing query text, plans, and runtime stats continuously across the fleet, and that data is the thing both of the other two systems actually depend on. Without it enabled and retained properly, Automatic Tuning has nothing to detect regressions against, and any job logic trying to make smart decisions about index health is working half-blind.

Automatic Tuning sits right on top of that as the automated first responder, specifically for plan regressions — force-last-good-plan reacting in near real time whenever Query Store's own data shows a query's new plan is measurably worse than its old one. That's the high-volume, low-judgment layer handled with zero human involvement.

Elastic Jobs is where I put the scheduled, fleet-wide maintenance that Automatic Tuning genuinely doesn't cover — actual index fragmentation checks and rebuilds, because a fragmented index can still get a perfectly good plan forced onto it and still perform badly on degraded physical structure. But the piece I think ties this whole thing together is having an Elastic Job specifically aggregate Automatic Tuning's own recommendation and action history across all 150 databases into one weekly report, instead of leaving a DBA to go check 150 databases' tuning dashboards one at a time.

That consolidated report is where the human intervention path actually lives — it's not a separate, disconnected process, it's built right on top of this pipeline. It flags databases where automatic tuning is firing unusually often, index recommendations that got surfaced but deliberately not auto-applied, and fragmentation that keeps coming back fast after a rebuild. That report becomes my actual prioritized worklist — I'm not hunting for problems across 150 databases, the automation hands me exactly the cases that need real judgment, while quietly handling everything routine on its own. That handoff — Query Store feeding Automatic Tuning, Automatic Tuning's history feeding into an Elastic Job's consolidated report, that report feeding the DBA — is the actual architecture, not three tools that happen to coexist.

Assuming Automatic Tuning's plan-forcing also resolves index fragmentation
Not building a mechanism to aggregate Automatic Tuning's fleet-wide history for human review
Leaving the DBA to manually check 150 databases individually rather than designing a consolidated report
Designing automation with no clear, documented path for when human judgment is actually needed
keyPoints: Query Store is the foundational data layer both Automatic Tuning and informed Elastic Job logic depend on
Automatic Tuning (FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN) acts as the near-real-time, no-human-needed first responder for plan regressions
Elastic Jobs handles scheduled fragmentation maintenance that Automatic Tuning's plan-forcing doesn't address
An Elastic Job should specifically aggregate Automatic Tuning's own history/recommendations fleet-wide into one report
The consolidated report is the documented, deliberate entry point for human intervention, not a disconnected process
The architecture is a deliberate pipeline/handoff between the three tools, not three independently-enabled features

Correctly explains Automatic Tuning's automated-response role and its limits
Correctly explains Elastic Jobs' role for fragmentation maintenance AND history aggregation

questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.
questions.example: Split: (1) Validate CLV calculation logic with Product, (2) Confirm/connect data sources, (3) Build semantic model & measures, (4) Build dashboard visualization — each separately estimated.
commonMistakes: Accepting a vague, oversized story as a single sprint item without decomposing it
Silently re-estimating the story unilaterally instead of involving the team
Publicly undermining the junior analyst's original estimate instead of framing it as a normal grooming gap
Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery
keyPoints: Decomposes a vague, oversized backlog item into independently valuable, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation and data-source unknowns during grooming, not mid-sprint
Reframes the original estimate's gap constructively rather than as a mistake by the junior analyst
Facilitates collaborative team re-estimation rather than overriding unilaterally
Models proactive unknown-surfacing as a senior responsibility within the Scrum process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and decomposes the oversized/ambiguous story into discrete, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation logic and data source unknowns proactively during grooming
Handles the junior analyst's original estimate constructively and respectfully
Uses collaborative, team-based re-estimation rather than unilateral override
Demonstrates understanding of how senior ownership operates within the Scrum process

questions.title: Why Wait Statistics Are the Starting Point, Not Resource Metrics
questions.prompt: A manager asks why your performance-tuning process starts with sys.dm_os_wait_stats instead of just watching CPU and memory counters in Task Manager or Performance Monitor. Explain what wait statistics actually measure that resource counters don't, how you'd use a wait-stats snapshot to decide where to spend your next hour of tuning time, and why you have to clear/baseline the waits before trusting the numbers.
questions.modelAnswer:
Resource counters tell you how busy a component is; wait statistics tell you what SQL Server's worker threads were actually blocked on while they weren't running your queries. CPU% or available memory can look perfectly healthy while queries are still slow because the real constraint is something counters don't expose directly -- lock waits, latch contention on a hot page, PAGEIOLATCH waits against a specific file, or threads queued behind MAXDOP on an overloaded scheduler. sys.dm_os_wait_stats aggregates, since the last restart or the last manual clear, the cumulative wait time by wait type across every worker thread, which converts 'the server feels slow' into a ranked list of exactly what SQL Server spent its time waiting on.

To decide where to spend the next hour, I'd snapshot the DMV, subtract out benign/background wait types that don't indicate a real problem (SLEEP_TASK, BROKER_TASK_STOP, XE_TIMER_EVENT, and similar), sort by wait_time_ms descending, and look at the top two or three categories as a percentage of total signal+resource wait time. A dominant CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER points at parallelism; dominant PAGEIOLATCH_SH/EX points at I/O against specific files; dominant LCK_M_* points at blocking; a high ratio of signal wait to resource wait points at CPU pressure itself (threads are runnable but waiting for a scheduler). That ranking is the actual prioritization tool -- it tells you which category of fix (indexing, I/O, concurrency, hardware) will move the needle, rather than guessing from a CPU graph.

Baselining matters because the DMV is cumulative since the last restart (or DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR)): a server that's been up for three months will show enormous absolute numbers dominated by history, not by what's happening right now. You take two snapshots separated by a known window (say, 15 minutes during the complaint period) and diff them, so the wait breakdown reflects that specific window rather than three months of accumulated noise.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the manager: resource counters answer 'is the box busy,' wait stats answer 'busy doing what, specifically.' You can have 40% CPU and still have users complaining, because the bottleneck might be blocking or disk latency on one file, neither of which shows up as 'CPU is high.' Wait stats are SQL Server's own running tally of every reason a worker thread sat idle instead of executing -- so instead of guessing from a graph, I get a ranked list: this percentage of wait time was locking, this percentage was I/O, this percentage was parallelism overhead.

In practice, my first move on any tuning engagement is to snapshot that DMV, filter out the wait types that are just background noise, and see what's actually dominant. If it's PAGEIOLATCH waits concentrated on one data file, I'm not touching indexes first -- I'm looking at storage and that file's I/O pattern. If it's lock waits, I'm looking at blocking chains and isolation levels, not disk. That ranking is literally how I decide what to work on first, and it keeps me from spending a day optimizing a query that was never the actual constraint.

And I'd flag the baseline issue specifically, because it trips people up: if you just query the DMV on a server that's been running for months, you're looking at history, not now. I always diff two time-boxed snapshots -- or clear the counters right before a reproduction window -- so what I'm prioritizing reflects the problem as it's happening today, not an accumulation that's dominated by some one-time event from weeks ago.
questions.example:
-- Snapshot, wait, diff pattern for a time-boxed window
SELECT wait_type, wait_time_ms, signal_wait_time_ms, waiting_tasks_count
INTO #waits_before FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT IN ('SLEEP_TASK','BROKER_TASK_STOP','XE_TIMER_EVENT','LAZYWRITER_SLEEP');
-- ... wait 15 minutes during the complaint window ...
SELECT b.wait_type,
       (a.wait_time_ms - b.wait_time_ms) AS delta_wait_ms
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats a
JOIN #waits_before b ON a.wait_type = b.wait_type
ORDER BY delta_wait_ms DESC;
commonMistakes: Tuning off CPU/memory graphs alone and missing blocking or I/O-specific bottlenecks
Reading cumulative wait stats since last restart as if they reflect the current problem
Not filtering out benign/background wait types before ranking
Treating the single top wait type as the whole story instead of looking at the top few as a percentage of total
Ignoring the signal-wait-to-resource-wait ratio, which separately indicates CPU scheduling pressure
keyPoints: Wait stats show what threads were blocked on, not just how busy a resource looked
sys.dm_os_wait_stats is cumulative and must be baselined/diffed over a time-boxed window
Dominant wait categories map to different fixes: locking, I/O, parallelism, CPU scheduling
Filtering benign wait types is required before the ranking means anything
Wait-stats-first is how tuning time gets prioritized instead of guessed at

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains what wait stats measure vs. resource counters
Describes using a ranked wait-stats snapshot to prioritize tuning work
Explains why baselining/diffing over a window is required
Connects at least two wait-type categories to their corresponding fix area
Clear, accurate, confidently delivered explanation

questions.title: Log Shipping vs. Database Mirroring: Why You'd Still Choose Either Over an Availability Group
questions.prompt: Always On Availability Groups get most of the attention, but a client with Standard Edition and a single reporting-only secondary asks you to justify using log shipping or mirroring instead. Compare log shipping and (legacy) database mirroring on failover automation, data currency, and licensing/edition requirements, and explain the specific scenario where you'd recommend log shipping over everything else, including an AG.
questions.modelAnswer:
Database mirroring is deprecated and Microsoft has said so for years, but it still shows up in older environments, and it offered something log shipping never did: near-real-time synchronization and automatic failover in high-safety mode with a witness, at the cost of being limited to one principal/one mirror pair and no readable secondary without a snapshot workaround. Log shipping, by contrast, is explicitly asynchronous and manual-failover by design -- it restores transaction log backups to one or more secondaries on a schedule (commonly every 5-15 minutes), so the secondary is always some controlled number of minutes behind, and bringing it online as the new primary is a deliberate, scripted action, not automatic.

On licensing/edition: this is the deciding factor as often as the technical behavior. Log shipping and mirroring both work on Standard Edition. Availability Groups in their full form (multiple secondaries, automatic failover, read-scale) require Enterprise Edition; Standard Edition only gets 'Basic Availability Groups,' which cap out at a single secondary, no readable secondary, and no multiple-database-per-group support -- functionally closer to mirroring than to a real AG. So for a Standard Edition client who specifically wants a secondary purely for offloaded reporting, log shipping is often the only Standard-Edition-compatible option that gives a readable secondary at all, since Basic AGs don't support readable secondaries either.

The scenario where I'd pick log shipping over an AG even when Enterprise Edition is available: a reporting-only secondary where you explicitly want a time-delayed, read-only copy -- for example, deliberately holding the secondary 30-60 minutes behind production as a safety net against an accidental mass delete or corruption propagating instantly to the DR copy. An AG's secondaries replay changes continuously (synchronously or near-synchronously), so a bad transaction on the primary reaches the secondary almost immediately; log shipping's restore delay is a feature there, not a limitation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk the client through it as a tradeoff table, not 'log shipping is worse.' Mirroring's selling point was automatic failover with a witness and almost no data loss in synchronous mode -- but it's deprecated, limited to a single mirror, and Microsoft's clearly pointed everyone toward AGs for years now, so I wouldn't actively recommend it for anything new. Log shipping is the one that's still genuinely useful: it's asynchronous by design, the secondary lags behind on a schedule you control, and bringing it online is a manual, deliberate step -- which sounds like a downside until you realize that's exactly what you want for a reporting copy or a deliberately time-delayed DR copy.

The licensing point is usually what actually settles it for a Standard Edition client. Full Always On Availability Groups -- multiple secondaries, automatic failover, a genuinely readable secondary -- are an Enterprise Edition feature. Standard Edition only gets Basic Availability Groups, and those don't even give you a readable secondary. So if this client is on Standard and wants a secondary they can run reports against, log shipping might be the only option on the table, not just the cheaper one.

And there's one case where I'd pick log shipping even with Enterprise Edition sitting right there: when the client explicitly wants delay. If someone fat-fingers a DELETE with no WHERE clause, an AG's secondary has that change almost instantly. A log-shipped secondary held 30-60 minutes behind is still clean when that happens, and that lag is the actual value proposition, not something to engineer around.
commonMistakes: Recommending AGs reflexively without checking the client's SQL Server edition
Not knowing Standard Edition's Basic Availability Groups lack a readable secondary
Treating log shipping's lag purely as a weakness instead of a deliberate safety feature
Recommending deprecated database mirroring for new implementations
Assuming automatic failover is always preferable, even for a reporting-only secondary that doesn't need it
keyPoints: Mirroring is deprecated; still relevant only in legacy environments
Log shipping is asynchronous with a controlled, scheduled restore delay and manual failover
Full Always On AGs require Enterprise Edition; Standard gets limited Basic AGs with no readable secondary
Log shipping is often the only Standard-Edition option for a readable secondary
Deliberate lag in log shipping protects against instantly-propagated mass deletes/corruption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately compares failover automation across all three technologies
Accurately compares data currency/lag behavior
Correctly explains edition/licensing constraints (Standard vs. Enterprise, Basic AGs)
Identifies a specific, valid scenario favoring log shipping over an AG
Clear, well-organized comparison

questions.title: Backup/Recovery Parity: Mapping SQL Server's Model onto Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
questions.prompt: A SQL Server DBA on your team is picking up Oracle responsibilities and keeps asking 'what's the RMAN equivalent of a differential backup?' Explain how Oracle RMAN, MySQL (mysqldump/XtraBackup/binary logs), and PostgreSQL (pg_dump/pg_basebackup/WAL archiving) each achieve the same three things SQL Server gives you natively -- full backups, incremental capture, and point-in-time recovery -- and call out the one platform where the terminology maps cleanly and the one where it doesn't.
questions.modelAnswer:
All four platforms solve the same three problems -- get a full copy, avoid re-copying everything every time, and recover to an arbitrary point between backups -- but land on different mechanisms. SQL Server's native model is full backup, differential backup (changed extents since the last full), and transaction log backups replayed for point-in-time recovery.

Oracle RMAN maps closest to that model conceptually but not in naming: a full RMAN backup backs up every used block; an incremental backup (level 1, cumulative or differential) captures changed blocks since a prior backup, which is RMAN's real analog to a SQL Server differential, not a straight rename. Point-in-time recovery comes from applying archived redo logs (and online redo) on top of a restored backup, directly analogous to replaying SQL Server transaction log backups -- redo logs are Oracle's transaction log.

MySQL splits cleanly into logical and physical: mysqldump produces a logical (SQL statement) full backup with no native differential concept, while Percona XtraBackup provides physical full and incremental backups comparable to RMAN/SQL Server differentials. Point-in-time recovery comes from replaying binary logs (binlogs) captured since the last backup -- MySQL's rough transaction-log equivalent, though binlogs are also the replication mechanism, which is a meaningfully different design choice than a dedicated transaction log.

PostgreSQL is the one where terminology diverges the most: pg_dump/pg_dumpall are logical backups with no true differential; pg_basebackup takes a physical full backup; there's no native 'differential backup' command at all -- continuous WAL archiving is instead combined with periodic full base backups, and point-in-time recovery is achieved by replaying WAL segments forward from a base backup to a target timestamp or LSN. So PostgreSQL gets PITR, but via continuous log shipping/archiving rather than anything resembling a SQL Server differential.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell them to stop looking for a one-to-one rename and think in terms of the three jobs any backup strategy does, because that's what actually transfers. Oracle's RMAN is the platform that maps closest: an RMAN incremental backup genuinely is the differential-backup idea, just captured at the block level and called something else, and archived redo logs play the exact role transaction log backups play for point-in-time recovery -- same job, different vocabulary.

MySQL is where I'd slow down, because 'backup' splits into two completely different tools with different capabilities: mysqldump is logical, basically a giant script of INSERT statements, and has no real differential concept at all. XtraBackup is the physical, incremental-capable tool that's actually comparable to a SQL Server differential. And point-in-time recovery comes from binlogs, which is MySQL's closest thing to a transaction log, except binlogs are also what replication runs on, which is a design choice SQL Server doesn't really have an equivalent of.

PostgreSQL is the one I'd flag as genuinely not mapping cleanly: there's no command called 'differential backup' at all. You get a physical full backup with pg_basebackup, and then point-in-time recovery comes from continuously archiving WAL segments and replaying them forward -- so PITR exists, it's just achieved through what's closer to continuous log shipping than to anything SQL Server calls a 'differential.' I'd tell a SQL Server DBA moving into Postgres to stop hunting for the differential-backup button, because there genuinely isn't one.
commonMistakes: Assuming every platform has a literal 'differential backup' feature by that name
Confusing MySQL's logical (mysqldump) and physical (XtraBackup) backup tools as interchangeable
Not recognizing MySQL binary logs serve both replication and point-in-time recovery
Expecting PostgreSQL to have a dedicated differential-backup command instead of WAL archiving
Treating RMAN incrementals as identical in mechanism to SQL Server differentials rather than analogous in purpose
keyPoints: All platforms solve: full backup, incremental capture, point-in-time recovery -- via different mechanisms
Oracle RMAN incrementals + archived redo logs map closest conceptually to SQL Server's model
MySQL splits into logical (mysqldump) vs. physical (XtraBackup) tools; binlogs drive PITR and replication
PostgreSQL has no native differential backup; PITR comes from WAL archiving plus periodic base backups
Terminology divergence is highest in PostgreSQL, closest in Oracle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps full/incremental/PITR concepts across all three platforms
Correctly identifies Oracle as the closest terminology match
Correctly identifies PostgreSQL as the least direct terminology match and explains why
Distinguishes MySQL's logical vs. physical backup tooling correctly
Clear, well-organized cross-platform comparison

questions.title: Consistency Models: MongoDB Read Concerns, Cosmos DB Consistency Levels, and Neo4j Clustering
questions.prompt: Explain, at a level a relational DBA moving into NoSQL would actually use on the job, how MongoDB's read/write concerns, Azure Cosmos DB's five consistency levels, and Neo4j Causal Clustering's read/write semantics each let you trade consistency for latency and availability -- and give one concrete scenario where you'd deliberately choose a weaker consistency setting over the strongest available one.
questions.modelAnswer:
All three systems expose the same underlying CAP-theorem tradeoff -- stronger consistency generally costs latency and/or availability during partitions -- but surface it through different knobs. MongoDB separates the choice into write concern (how many replica set members must acknowledge a write before it's considered successful: w:1, w:majority, or a specific number/tag set) and read concern (what a read is allowed to see: local, available, majority, or linearizable). A w:majority write combined with a majority or linearizable read gives strong, durable consistency across a replica set failover; w:1 with local reads is faster but can read back data that a failover later rolls back.

Cosmos DB makes this explicit as five named levels on a spectrum: strong (linearizable, every region sees the same data, highest latency/lowest availability under partition), bounded staleness (lag bounded by time or operation count), session (strong consistency within a single client session, the default and most commonly used), consistent prefix, and eventual (lowest latency, no ordering guarantee). Because Cosmos DB is designed for global multi-region distribution, the practical default for most applications is session consistency -- strong enough for a user to always see their own writes, without paying the cross-region latency cost of strong consistency on every request.

Neo4j Causal Clustering guarantees causal consistency: a client that writes through the cluster and then reads is guaranteed to see that write (via a bookmark passed from the write transaction to the subsequent read), even though follower/read-replica reads in general can lag the leader. You can still read from a replica that hasn't caught up if you don't pass the bookmark, trading strict freshness for read scalability across replicas.

Concrete scenario for choosing weaker consistency deliberately: a product-catalog read path serving millions of read-only requests where a few seconds of staleness is invisible to the business (price updates are rare and non-urgent) -- eventual consistency in Cosmos DB, or local read concern against secondaries in MongoDB, cuts latency and cost substantially with no real downside, versus paying strong/linearizable consistency costs on every catalog page view.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame it as: every one of these systems is really just giving you a dial between 'definitely consistent, possibly slower or less available' and 'fast and available, possibly stale,' and the job is picking the right point on that dial per use case, not defaulting to the strongest setting everywhere out of caution.

MongoDB does it with two separate knobs -- write concern decides how many nodes have to confirm a write before you call it done, read concern decides what guarantees a read gets. w:majority plus majority or linearizable reads is your 'this really happened and won't get rolled back' setting; w:1 with local reads is fast but can show you something a failover later undoes.

Cosmos DB just names the whole spectrum for you -- strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, eventual -- and in practice almost everyone defaults to session consistency, because it guarantees you always see your own writes without paying the latency cost of making every single region agree on every single request, which is what strong consistency demands in a globally distributed system.

Neo4j's Causal Clustering guarantees you'll see your own writes if you carry the bookmark from the write into the next read, but a plain read against a follower can lag behind, which is fine for scaling out read traffic as long as you're deliberate about when you need that guarantee and when you don't.

Where I'd deliberately go weaker: a product catalog or content feed getting read-heavy traffic where staleness of a few seconds is genuinely invisible to the user. Paying strong-consistency latency on every page view of a catalog that updates prices once a day is just burning money and response time for a guarantee nobody needed.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'strongest consistency' is always the safest default regardless of workload
Confusing MongoDB write concern (durability of the write) with read concern (visibility guarantees on reads)
Not knowing Cosmos DB session consistency is the practical default, not strong
Assuming Neo4j Causal Clustering reads are always fully consistent without understanding bookmarks
Ignoring the latency/cost tradeoff that strong consistency imposes in globally distributed systems
keyPoints: All three expose a consistency-vs-latency/availability tradeoff rooted in CAP theorem
MongoDB: write concern (durability) and read concern (visibility) are separate, composable settings
Cosmos DB: five named consistency levels, session is the common default
Neo4j Causal Clustering: bookmarks guarantee read-your-writes; unbookmarked replica reads can lag
Weaker consistency is the right choice for high-volume, staleness-tolerant read paths

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains MongoDB read/write concern options
Correctly explains Cosmos DB's five consistency levels and the common default
Correctly explains Neo4j Causal Clustering consistency semantics and bookmarks
Gives a concrete, valid scenario for deliberately choosing weaker consistency
Clear, accurate, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Writing a DMV Query to Rank Wait Types for a Specific Database
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against sys.dm_os_wait_stats that excludes common benign/background wait types, and shows the top 10 wait types by total wait time along with each one's percentage of total resource wait time. Then explain how you'd adapt this into a repeatable baseline-and-diff script for a scheduled health check.
questions.code:
SELECT TOP 10
    wait_type,
    wait_time_ms,
    waiting_tasks_count,
    CAST(100.0 * wait_time_ms / SUM(wait_time_ms) OVER() AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS pct_of_total
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT IN (
    'SLEEP_TASK','BROKER_TASK_STOP','BROKER_TO_FLUSH','XE_TIMER_EVENT',
    'LAZYWRITER_SLEEP','CLR_SEMAPHORE','SQLTRACE_BUFFER_FLUSH',
    'WAITFOR','CHECKPOINT_QUEUE','REQUEST_FOR_DEADLOCK_SEARCH',
    'XE_DISPATCHER_WAIT','FT_IFTS_SCHEDULER_IDLE_WAIT','DIRTY_PAGE_POLL'
)
AND waiting_tasks_count > 0
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
questions.modelAnswer:
The query above filters sys.dm_os_wait_stats down to wait types with at least one waiting task (so I don't rank wait types that have never actually blocked anything), excludes the standard list of benign background waits that always accumulate on an idle instance and add noise, and uses a window function (SUM(...) OVER()) to compute each wait type's share of total resource wait time in the same pass, rather than a separate subquery. Ranking by raw wait_time_ms alone can be misleading on a server that's been up a long time, so showing the percentage of total gives a sense of whether the top wait type is genuinely dominant (60%+) or whether the waits are spread thin across many types (nothing above 10-15%), which itself is diagnostic information -- a flat distribution often means there isn't one obvious bottleneck.

To turn this into a repeatable baseline-and-diff health check, I'd capture the full (unfiltered, so nothing is lost) result of sys.dm_os_wait_stats into a permanent logging table on a schedule via SQL Server Agent -- say every 15 or 30 minutes -- tagged with a capture timestamp. A second step computes the delta between consecutive snapshots for each wait type (today's cumulative value minus the prior snapshot's cumulative value), which gives the wait time accrued in just that interval rather than since the last restart. That delta table is what the top-10 percentage query above should actually run against for a scheduled health check, because it reflects 'what happened in the last 15-30 minutes,' which is the actionable, current signal -- not lifetime totals that get harder to interpret the longer the instance has been up.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through what I wrote: I filter out waiting_tasks_count = 0 rows and the standard benign-wait blocklist first, because otherwise you're ranking noise alongside real signal, and I compute percent-of-total with a window function so I get the ranking and the share in one query instead of two. The percentage matters more than people expect -- if the top wait type is 70% of total wait time, that's your bottleneck, full stop; if the top five are all under 12%, that tells you there isn't a single dominant issue and you need to look elsewhere, maybe at specific queries rather than instance-wide waits.

For turning it into an actual scheduled health check, the key design decision is: don't query this DMV directly in your scheduled job and trust the raw numbers, because they're cumulative since the last restart. I'd build a small logging table, have an Agent job insert a full snapshot of sys.dm_os_wait_stats into it every 15-30 minutes with a timestamp, and then compute deltas between consecutive rows per wait type. That delta is the number that actually means something on an ongoing basis -- it tells you what accumulated in the last interval, so if something spikes, you catch it in that run instead of it getting buried in months of history. I'd keep the raw snapshot table trimmed with a retention job too, since it grows every interval forever otherwise.
commonMistakes: Ranking by raw wait_time_ms without excluding benign background wait types
Not filtering out wait types with zero waiting_tasks_count
Running the query directly against the live DMV for a scheduled report instead of logging snapshots and diffing
Forgetting the DMV is cumulative since the last restart, making lifetime totals hard to interpret
Not adding a retention/cleanup step to a growing logging table
keyPoints: Filter benign wait types and zero-count rows before ranking
Window functions can compute percent-of-total in the same query as the ranking
A flat wait distribution is itself diagnostic (no single dominant bottleneck)
A health check needs logged snapshots and interval deltas, not raw cumulative DMV reads
Retention/cleanup is required for any logging table used this way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Query correctly filters benign wait types and zero-count rows
Query correctly computes and ranks by percentage of total wait time
Explains the baseline-and-diff pattern for a scheduled job
Notes the need for a logging table plus retention/cleanup
Clean, correct, readable T-SQL

questions.title: Standing Up Ola Hallengren's Maintenance Scripts as Scheduled Agent Jobs
questions.prompt: Walk through, with actual commands, how you'd install Ola Hallengren's maintenance solution on a production instance and schedule it as three separate SQL Server Agent jobs (index/stats optimization, integrity checks, backups) with sane parameters, instead of relying on the built-in Maintenance Plan wizard. Explain the specific parameter choices you'd make for the index optimization job on a large, actively-written-to database.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd avoid the Maintenance Plan wizard entirely for anything beyond the smallest environments, because it can't make an online-vs-offline rebuild decision based on actual fragmentation thresholds, can't skip statistics that haven't changed, and gives much weaker logging than Ola's scripts. The install itself is just running his MaintenanceSolution.sql script in a DBA administration database (or master), which creates the stored procedures (CommandExecute, DatabaseBackup, IndexOptimize, Output File Cleanup) and, if you let it, the Agent jobs automatically -- though I usually review and re-create the jobs by hand so the schedules and parameters are deliberate rather than defaults.

For the index optimization job on a large, actively-written-to database, the parameter choices that matter: @FragmentationLow left alone (don't touch indexes below the low threshold at all, usually 5-10%, since rebuilding barely-fragmented indexes wastes I/O for no benefit); @FragmentationMedium set to REORGANIZE first, with REBUILD as a fallback, for the mid-range (commonly 10-30%) since reorganize is lighter-weight and mostly online; @FragmentationHigh set straight to REBUILD_ONLINE where Enterprise Edition and no LOB columns make that possible, since high fragmentation (30%+) on a big table needs the real fix, not a reorganize. @UpdateStatistics = 'ALL' combined with @OnlyModifiedStatistics = 'Y' updates statistics even on indexes that weren't touched by the fragmentation pass, but only the ones that actually changed, which keeps the job from re-scanning statistics that are already current. Critically, I'd set @TimeLimit to cap the job's total runtime so it can't run into business hours on a bad night, and @LogToTable = 'Y' so every run is captured in the CommandLog table for troubleshooting and trend analysis, not just whatever's in the Agent job history.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My answer to 'why not just use the Maintenance Plan wizard' is always the same: it's fine for a tiny single-database shop, and it falls apart fast on anything real, because it doesn't do threshold-based decisions -- it just rebuilds or reorganizes everything on the schedule you give it, which either wastes resources on indexes that didn't need it or under-serves ones that desperately did. Ola's scripts are the de facto industry standard specifically because IndexOptimize makes that low/medium/high fragmentation decision for you, per index, every run.

Installing it is the easy part -- run the script, get the procedures, set up three Agent jobs calling DatabaseBackup, dbo.IndexOptimize, and the integrity-check procedure on separate schedules (backups most frequently, index optimization during a maintenance window, integrity checks maybe weekly since CHECKDB is expensive).

The parameter choices are where the judgment is. On a big, busy table, I don't want REBUILD running at the low fragmentation tier at all -- that's pure waste. I want REORGANIZE as the first option in the medium tier because it's lighter and mostly online, with REBUILD_ONLINE as the real fix once fragmentation gets serious, assuming we're on an edition and table structure that supports online rebuilds. I always turn on @LogToTable, because when someone asks six weeks later 'did maintenance actually run last Tuesday,' I want a table to query, not a guess based on Agent job history retention. And I always cap @TimeLimit, because an uncapped maintenance job that's still rebuilding indexes at 8am on a Monday is a much worse outcome than one that stopped partway through and picked up where it left off the next night.
commonMistakes: Relying on the built-in Maintenance Plan wizard for a large or heavily-written-to production database
Rebuilding every index on a fixed schedule regardless of actual fragmentation level
Not setting @TimeLimit, risking maintenance jobs running into business hours
Not enabling @LogToTable, losing the ability to audit or trend maintenance history
Forgetting that online rebuilds require Enterprise Edition and have restrictions with certain column types
keyPoints: Ola Hallengren's scripts make threshold-based rebuild/reorganize decisions the wizard cannot
Low fragmentation should be left alone; medium favors reorganize; high favors rebuild
@OnlyModifiedStatistics avoids wasted work on unchanged statistics
@TimeLimit protects business hours from runaway maintenance jobs
@LogToTable is required for auditability and troubleshooting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Ola's scripts are preferred over the Maintenance Plan wizard
Correctly describes the install and Agent job setup process
Justifies fragmentation threshold parameter choices (low/medium/high)
Explains @TimeLimit, @LogToTable, and @OnlyModifiedStatistics choices
Clear, technically accurate, production-minded answer

questions.title: Writing a dbatools Pipeline to Back Up and Verify Every Database Across a Server List
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell script using dbatools that reads a list of SQL Server instances, takes a full backup of every user database on each one, and verifies the backup actually succeeded before moving to the next instance -- with error handling so one failed instance doesn't stop the whole run. Explain the error-handling pattern you used and why it matters at scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
The script loops instances, and within each instance loops its user databases, using Get-DbaDatabase, Backup-DbaDatabase, and Test-DbaLastBackup -- that last one actually restores the backup to a scratch location and runs integrity checks against it, which is the real verification step; a backup command returning success only tells you the backup operation completed, not that the resulting file is restorable.

The error-handling pattern is two nested try/catch blocks, not one. The outer catch handles an entire instance being unreachable (connection failure, instance down, permissions problem) and records that as a single failure row without ever touching its databases. The inner catch handles a single database's backup or verification failing without affecting any other database on that same instance, or any other instance in the list. This matters at scale specifically because a flat, single try/catch around the whole script would mean one unreachable instance, or one corrupt database that fails verification, stops the entire run -- so every instance after the failure point silently never gets backed up that night, and you might not notice until someone needs a restore. With nested, scoped error handling, a bad instance or database becomes one row in a results log instead of a run-ending exception, and every other instance still gets processed.

Every outcome -- success or failure -- gets written to a structured results array rather than just printed to the console, which is what makes the Export-CSV and the failure-count email at the end possible; you can't alert on failures you never captured as data.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I'd walk an interviewer through first is: don't wrap the whole script in one try/catch, because that turns 'instance #3 of 40 is down tonight' into 'nothing from instance #3 onward got backed up, and nobody finds out until it's too late.' I scope error handling at two levels -- per instance, and per database within that instance -- so a failure anywhere stays contained to the smallest unit that actually failed, and the loop just keeps going.

The verification step is the other thing people skip and shouldn't: Backup-DbaDatabase succeeding just means SQL Server wrote a file. Test-DbaLastBackup actually restores that backup somewhere and runs a consistency check against it, which is the only way to know the backup is real and usable, not just present. I've seen plenty of 'backups' that were technically completing every night onto a share with a permissions issue that silently truncated the files -- you don't catch that without an actual restore test.

I also made sure every result, success or failure, becomes a row in a PSCustomObject collection instead of console output, because that's what lets me export a CSV for an audit trail and build a failure-count alert at the end. At 40+ instances a night, nobody's watching the console in real time -- the whole point of automating this is that a human only needs to look at it when the automated run is telling them something's actually wrong.
commonMistakes: Wrapping the entire multi-instance loop in a single try/catch, letting one failure stop the whole run
Treating a successful Backup-DbaDatabase call as proof the backup is restorable
Not capturing results as structured data, making alerting/reporting impossible
Hardcoding the instance list instead of reading it from an external, maintainable source
Not separating instance-level connection failures from database-level backup failures in the error log
keyPoints: Nested try/catch scopes failures to the instance or database level, not the whole run
Test-DbaLastBackup provides real verification via restore + consistency check, not just backup success
Structured result objects enable CSV export and automated failure alerting
One bad instance or database should never silently prevent others from being backed up
Error handling at scale is about containment, not prevention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Script correctly backs up all user databases across a list of instances
Includes genuine backup verification (restore-based), not just backup success
Error handling is scoped (per-instance and per-database) so failures don't halt the run
Explains why this error-handling pattern matters at scale
Results are captured as structured data enabling logging/alerting

questions.title: Setting Up PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery with pg_basebackup and WAL Archiving
questions.prompt: Walk through, with actual commands and configuration settings, how you'd set up continuous WAL archiving and take a physical base backup of a PostgreSQL instance so that you can restore to an arbitrary point in time later. Then describe the actual recovery steps you'd take to restore to 2:47pm after an accidental mass UPDATE at 3:00pm.
questions.code:
# postgresql.conf
wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'cp %p /mnt/wal_archive/%f'

# Take the physical base backup
pg_basebackup -h localhost -U replicator -D /mnt/backups/base_2026_10_09 -Fp -Xs -P

# --- After the accidental 3:00pm mass UPDATE ---
# 1. Stop PostgreSQL, preserve current data dir for forensics, restore base backup
systemctl stop postgresql
mv /var/lib/postgresql/16/main /var/lib/postgresql/16/main_bad
cp -R /mnt/backups/base_2026_10_09 /var/lib/postgresql/16/main

# 2. recovery signal + target time (PostgreSQL 12+)
touch /var/lib/postgresql/16/main/recovery.signal
cat >> /var/lib/postgresql/16/main/postgresql.conf <<EOF
restore_command = 'cp /mnt/wal_archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-09 14:47:00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'
EOF

# 3. Start PostgreSQL -- it replays WAL up to the target time, then promotes
systemctl start postgresql
questions.modelAnswer:
WAL archiving has to be turned on before you need it -- it's not something you enable retroactively once you need point-in-time recovery, because PITR depends on having an unbroken chain of archived WAL segments from the base backup forward. wal_level = replica ensures enough information is written to WAL to support replay; archive_mode = on plus an archive_command (here, a simple copy to a separate archive location, though production setups more commonly use a tool like pgBackRest or WAL-G and often ship to object storage) is what actually preserves each completed WAL segment instead of letting PostgreSQL recycle it.

pg_basebackup takes a physical, restorable copy of the whole data directory at a point in time; -Xs streams the WAL generated during the backup itself so the backup is self-consistent, and -P shows progress. That base backup plus every WAL segment archived after it together form the full recoverable timeline.

For the actual recovery to 2:47pm after a 3:00pm mass UPDATE: stop the instance, move the damaged data directory aside rather than deleting it (so there's a forensic copy if something goes wrong with the restore), and replace the data directory with a fresh copy of the base backup. Creating recovery.signal (PostgreSQL 12+; standby.signal is for replicas, recovery.signal is for PITR) tells PostgreSQL to enter recovery mode on startup rather than normal startup. Setting restore_command tells it how to fetch archived WAL segments it needs, recovery_target_time gives the exact stopping point, and recovery_target_action = 'promote' tells it to come out of recovery and become a normal, writable primary once it reaches that target rather than pausing. Starting the service then replays WAL from the base backup forward, stops exactly at 2:47pm -- before the 3:00pm UPDATE was ever written -- and promotes to a live, usable database.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I'd emphasize first, because it trips up people coming from SQL Server: you cannot retroactively recover to a point in time if WAL archiving wasn't already running before the incident. SQL Server DBAs are used to transaction log backups being something you can reason about after the fact if the recovery model was right; PostgreSQL PITR specifically requires that unbroken WAL archive chain to already exist, so this has to be set up as standard practice on day one, not reached for during an incident.

Given that it was already running, my recovery playbook is: don't touch or delete the damaged data directory, move it aside instead, because if the restore goes wrong or someone wants to do forensics on exactly what that bad UPDATE did, you want that evidence intact. Then it's a fresh copy of the base backup into the data directory, a recovery.signal file to tell Postgres 'don't start up normally, go into recovery,' a restore_command so it knows how to pull WAL segments from the archive, and recovery_target_time set to 2:47pm with recovery_target_action set to promote so it doesn't just pause at that point and wait for a manual command -- it comes up live and usable automatically once it reaches the target.

One thing I always double- and triple-check in a real incident: get the target time right and a little conservative. If the bad UPDATE started at 3:00pm sharp, I'd target comfortably before that, verify the data looks right once it's promoted, and only then treat the recovery as done -- getting the target time wrong by even a minute in the wrong direction either loses good data or keeps the bad update.
commonMistakes: Trying to enable WAL archiving after an incident instead of having it running beforehand
Deleting or overwriting the damaged data directory instead of preserving it for forensics
Confusing standby.signal (for replicas) with recovery.signal (for point-in-time recovery)
Setting an imprecise recovery_target_time without verifying the data after promotion
Forgetting -Xs on pg_basebackup, risking a base backup that isn't self-consistent
keyPoints: WAL archiving (archive_mode, archive_command) must be running before PITR is possible
pg_basebackup plus archived WAL segments together form the recoverable timeline
recovery.signal plus restore_command and recovery_target_time drive PITR on startup
recovery_target_action = 'promote' brings the instance up live once the target is reached
Always preserve the damaged data directory rather than overwriting it during recovery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures WAL archiving settings before the incident
Correctly uses pg_basebackup to take a restorable physical backup
Correctly describes the recovery.signal / restore_command / recovery_target_time steps
Notes preserving the damaged data directory and verifying data post-recovery
Technically accurate, properly sequenced recovery procedure

questions.title: Choosing a MongoDB Shard Key for a Multi-Tenant SaaS Workload
questions.prompt: A MongoDB collection stores usage events for a multi-tenant SaaS product: {tenantId, userId, eventType, timestamp, payload}. Writes are heavy and roughly evenly spread across ~2,000 tenants, but a handful of large enterprise tenants generate 100x the events of a typical tenant. Propose a shard key, explain why a naive choice (tenantId alone, or timestamp alone) would create problems, and show the sharding commands you'd use to implement your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
tenantId alone would be a bad shard key here because of the skew described: a handful of enterprise tenants generate 100x the events of a typical tenant, which means all of that tenant's data lands on whatever single chunk/shard range owns that tenantId value -- creating a 'jumbo chunk' that MongoDB can't split further (a chunk is split on ranges of the shard key, and if one shard key value dominates the chunk, splitting doesn't rebalance it), and a hot shard that absorbs a disproportionate share of writes while other shards sit comparatively idle.

timestamp alone is worse in a different way: since timestamp is monotonically increasing, every single insert across every tenant targets the current 'latest' chunk, which lives on one shard at a time. That turns the busiest possible write pattern -- inserts happening right now, from every tenant simultaneously -- into traffic against a single shard, completely defeating the purpose of sharding for write scalability.

The fix is a compound shard key: { tenantId: 1, userId: "hashed" }. Keeping tenantId as the leading (range) component means queries that filter by tenant -- which is almost every query in a multi-tenant system, since tenants only ever query their own data -- can be targeted to the right range without a broadcast scatter-gather query across all shards. Hashing userId as the second component distributes each large tenant's own writes across many chunks and shards instead of concentrating them, which solves the big-tenant skew problem specifically: even though that enterprise tenant generates 100x the volume, its writes get spread across the hashed userId space rather than piling onto one chunk. Monitoring chunk distribution after rollout (sh.status(), or Atlas's built-in sharding metrics) is still necessary, because even this key benefits from watching for any secondary skew within a single giant tenant's own user population.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through why each naive option fails before proposing the fix, because the reasoning is the part that actually matters in an interview. tenantId by itself concentrates every one of those 100x-volume enterprise tenants onto a single chunk range -- and MongoDB can keep splitting a chunk as it grows, but it can't split a chunk below the level of distinct shard key values, so a tenant that's itself huge becomes a jumbo chunk that can't be broken up and can't be rebalanced off whatever shard it landed on. That's a hot-shard problem baked permanently into the design.

timestamp alone is actually the more common mistake people make with event/log-style collections, and it's subtly worse: because it's monotonically increasing, literally every insert from literally every tenant, at any given moment, is targeting the same 'current' chunk on the same single shard. You've built a system designed to scale writes that funnels 100% of current write traffic through one shard anyway.

What I'd actually deploy is a compound key -- tenantId leading, userId hashed. Leading with tenantId keeps per-tenant queries targeted instead of fanning out to every shard, which matters because in a multi-tenant system almost every query already has 'WHERE tenantId = X' built in. Hashing userId underneath it breaks up the big tenants' own write volume across the cluster instead of letting it pile onto one chunk. And I'd be upfront that this isn't 'set it and forget it' -- I'd still watch chunk distribution after rollout, because even a well-chosen key can develop secondary hot spots if, say, one user within a giant tenant becomes unusually active.
commonMistakes: Choosing tenantId alone and creating an unsplittable jumbo chunk for large tenants
Choosing timestamp alone and funneling all current writes to a single shard
Not recognizing that most queries in a multi-tenant system filter by tenant, making a targeted (non-hashed) leading component valuable
Hashing the entire compound key, losing the ability to target queries by tenant
Assuming the chosen shard key never needs post-rollout monitoring for secondary skew
keyPoints: A single highly-skewed value in a shard key creates an unsplittable, unbalanceable jumbo chunk
Monotonically increasing shard keys funnel all current writes to one shard
A compound key with a targeted leading field and a hashed trailing field balances query targeting and write distribution
tenantId as the leading key supports the common 'query within one tenant' access pattern
Shard key choice still requires ongoing monitoring for secondary skew within large partitions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why tenantId alone causes a jumbo-chunk/hot-shard problem
Correctly explains why timestamp alone funnels writes to a single shard
Proposes a valid compound shard key solving both problems
Correct sharding commands/syntax
Notes the need for ongoing monitoring of chunk/shard distribution

questions.title: Designing an Always On Availability Group Across Two Datacenters
questions.prompt: Design an Always On Availability Group spanning a primary datacenter and a secondary datacenter 40 miles away, supporting automatic failover for HA within the primary site and a DR copy in the secondary site, with a reporting workload that must not impact the primary. Specify replica count, synchronization modes, failover modes, listener/quorum considerations, and justify each choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd design a three-replica topology: two synchronous replicas in the primary datacenter (the primary itself plus one local synchronous secondary) configured for automatic failover, and one asynchronous replica in the secondary datacenter 40 miles away configured as a manual-failover DR copy, with the reporting workload directed at the local synchronous secondary rather than the DR replica.

Synchronization mode: the two in-datacenter replicas use synchronous commit specifically because automatic failover requires it -- SQL Server will not automatically fail over to an asynchronous replica, since asynchronous means the secondary could be meaningfully behind and an automatic failover to it could silently lose committed transactions. The cross-datacenter replica stays asynchronous because synchronous commit across a 40-mile link adds commit latency to every transaction on the primary (every write waits for acknowledgment from every synchronous replica), and that latency cost isn't justified for a DR copy that's meant for disaster recovery, not instant failover.

Failover mode: automatic failover between the two primary-datacenter replicas (protecting against a single server/VM failure without a human in the loop at 3am); manual failover to the DR replica, because failing over across datacenters has bigger blast-radius implications -- network/DNS/application connection-string considerations, and because async replication means a manual failover there requires a deliberate decision about accepting potential data loss (the RPO gap), which should never happen automatically.

Listener/quorum: the Windows Server Failover Cluster needs a quorum model that accounts for the cross-site asynchronous replica without letting it count toward automatic-failover quorum decisions that should only involve the two local synchronous replicas -- in practice this often means a File Share Witness or Cloud Witness placed in a third, independent location (not either datacenter) so a single-site outage doesn't itself create a split-brain or quorum-loss scenario. The reporting workload reads from the local synchronous secondary with read-only routing, isolating report-query resource consumption from the primary without adding cross-datacenter latency to reports, and without risking DR-replica staleness showing up in reports.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by separating the two problems this design actually has to solve, because they need different technology choices: HA within the primary site needs automatic failover and zero data loss, DR to the second site needs to survive losing the whole primary datacenter and doesn't need to be instant.

For HA, two replicas in the primary datacenter, both synchronous, with automatic failover between them -- that's the only way to get a no-data-loss, no-human-required failover for a single-server failure. For DR, one asynchronous replica 40 miles away with manual failover only. I'm deliberate about asynchronous there: making that link synchronous would mean every single transaction on the primary has to wait for an acknowledgment to travel 40 miles round-trip before it's considered committed, which is a real latency tax I'm not willing to pay for a replica that exists for disaster scenarios, not day-to-day failover.

Manual failover to the DR site isn't a limitation, it's deliberate -- crossing datacenters means dealing with DNS, application connection strings, and possibly accepting some data loss since the replica's asynchronous, and that's a decision a human should make with eyes open, not something that triggers automatically at 3am based on a monitoring false positive.

The quorum piece is the part people get wrong: I'd put a witness in a third location, independent of either datacenter, so quorum decisions for the automatic-failover pair aren't compromised by whatever's happening at either site, and so losing one datacenter doesn't also take out the thing deciding who's allowed to become primary.

And reporting goes against the local synchronous secondary with read-only routing -- that keeps report query load off the primary without adding 40 miles of latency to every report, and without ever reporting off data that might be lagging behind on the DR copy.
commonMistakes: Configuring automatic failover to an asynchronous cross-datacenter replica, risking silent data loss
Making the cross-datacenter replica synchronous and absorbing unnecessary commit latency on every transaction
Placing the quorum witness inside one of the two datacenters instead of a third, independent location
Directing reporting workload at the DR replica, risking stale data and cross-datacenter latency
Treating automatic failover as always the preferable choice regardless of distance/replication mode
keyPoints: Automatic failover requires synchronous commit; never pair automatic failover with an async replica
Cross-datacenter replicas should typically be asynchronous to avoid commit-latency cost on the primary
Manual failover is the deliberate, correct choice for cross-site DR failover
Quorum witness placement in a third, independent location prevents split-brain/quorum-loss on single-site failure
Read-only routing to a local secondary isolates reporting load without cross-site latency or staleness

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs replica count, placement, and sync modes
Correctly justifies automatic vs. manual failover choices
Addresses quorum/witness placement correctly
Correctly isolates the reporting workload without risking primary performance or data staleness
Clear, well-reasoned, production-grade architecture explanation

questions.title: Assessing a SQL Server-to-PostgreSQL Migration for a Mid-Sized Application
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to evaluate migrating a mid-sized OLTP application off SQL Server onto PostgreSQL to reduce licensing costs. As the architect for this assessment, outline the categories of risk you'd evaluate before committing to a migration plan -- covering T-SQL-specific feature dependencies, data type/schema conversion, and operational tooling parity -- and identify the single biggest hidden-cost category that non-DBAs on the leadership team are likely to underestimate.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd structure the assessment into four risk categories. First, T-SQL-specific feature dependencies: anything relying on SQL Server-specific surface area -- CLR integration, SQL Server Agent jobs with T-SQL job steps, linked servers, specific system functions, MERGE statement nuances, computed columns with specific behaviors, or heavy use of proprietary hints -- needs an inventory, because each either has a PostgreSQL equivalent requiring a rewrite, or has no clean equivalent and needs an architectural workaround (e.g., pg_cron or external schedulers replacing SQL Agent, FDWs or application-level logic replacing linked servers).

Second, data type and schema conversion: SQL Server and PostgreSQL diverge on things like IDENTITY vs. SERIAL/GENERATED AS IDENTITY, DATETIME2 vs. TIMESTAMP precision and time zone handling, NVARCHAR/collation behavior vs. PostgreSQL's text handling and collation model, and T-SQL's case-insensitive-by-default string comparisons vs. PostgreSQL's case-sensitive default -- that last one alone can silently break application queries and comparisons that worked by accident under SQL Server's default collation.

Third, operational tooling parity: does the organization have PostgreSQL-equivalent tooling for everything they currently depend on in the SQL Server ecosystem -- monitoring (replacing SQL Server-specific DMV-based dashboards), backup/HA tooling (pgBackRest or similar replacing native backup + Always On), and crucially, whether the existing DBA team has PostgreSQL operational depth or needs training/hiring.

Fourth, and this is the one leadership chronically underestimates: application-layer rewrite cost, specifically the ORM/data-access-layer and stored-procedure logic that assumes T-SQL syntax and behavior. Leadership tends to price a migration as 'database cost,' but the actual largest line item is almost always developer time rewriting and re-testing every stored procedure, every dynamically-built query, and every piece of application code that made T-SQL-specific assumptions -- plus the QA cycle needed to catch behavioral differences (like the case-sensitivity issue above) that don't throw an error, they just silently return wrong results.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd present this to leadership as four buckets, because 'is this feasible' and 'what does this actually cost' need different lenses. Feature dependencies first -- I'd want an actual inventory of what T-SQL-specific surface area we're using: SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, CLR, anything that's SQL-Server-only. Every item on that list is either 'there's a Postgres equivalent, budget the rewrite' or 'there's no clean equivalent, budget an architecture change.'

Data type and schema conversion is bucket two, and the one landmine I'd flag specifically in that meeting is collation and case sensitivity -- SQL Server's default is case-insensitive string comparison, PostgreSQL's default isn't, and that's the kind of difference that doesn't throw an error during migration, it just quietly returns different results in production weeks later, which is a much scarier failure mode than a migration script erroring out.

Tooling parity is bucket three -- do we have monitoring, backup, and HA tooling for Postgres, and does our DBA team already know it or do we need training and ramp-up time built into the timeline.

But if I had to point at the one thing leadership is going to underestimate, it's not any of those -- it's application and stored-procedure rewrite cost. They're going to price this as 'database migration,' and the real cost is almost entirely developer time: every stored procedure written in T-SQL, every ORM query that assumed SQL Server syntax or behavior, every piece of business logic sitting in the database layer, all of it needs to be rewritten and then QA'd thoroughly enough to catch silent behavioral differences, not just syntax errors. That's the line item that turns a 'should be straightforward' migration into a multi-quarter project, and it's the number I'd make sure is in the first slide, not buried in an appendix.
commonMistakes: Treating the migration as purely a database-engine swap rather than an application rewrite project
Not inventorying T-SQL-specific feature dependencies (Agent, linked servers, CLR) before committing to a timeline
Overlooking the case-sensitivity/collation default difference as a source of silent production bugs
Underestimating QA/regression testing effort needed to catch behavioral (not just syntax) differences
Assuming the existing DBA team has PostgreSQL operational depth without verifying or budgeting training
keyPoints: T-SQL-specific feature dependencies (Agent, linked servers, CLR) need a full inventory before committing
Data type/collation differences, especially case sensitivity, cause silent behavioral bugs, not errors
Operational tooling and DBA team skill parity must be assessed, not assumed
Application/stored-procedure rewrite and QA cost is the dominant, most underestimated cost category
Migration risk assessment must separate feasibility from true cost before a plan is committed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Covers T-SQL-specific feature dependency risk thoroughly
Covers data type/schema/collation conversion risk, including case sensitivity
Covers operational tooling and team-skill parity risk
Correctly identifies application/stored-procedure rewrite cost as the biggest underestimated cost
Clear, leadership-appropriate framing of technical risk
